panels.visual: Achilles in a fury over his friend's funeral pyre, golden hair, burning eyes, a spear in hand
panels.caption: The Trojan prince Hector killed Achilles' best friend Patroclus.

panels.visual: Achilles and Hector facing each other in a duel beneath the walls of Troy, dust swirl, shield and spear clashes, no gore
panels.caption: Achilles went out to meet Hector in single combat outside the walls.

panels.visual: Achilles' chariot racing around the walls of Troy, a billow of dust trailing behind it, Hector's parents on the battlements with hands to their mouths
panels.caption: He dragged Hector round the walls of Troy for days. Nobody stopped him.

panels.visual: Old King Priam kneeling in Achilles' tent with a gentle expression, Achilles weeping with him, lamp glow
panels.caption: One night old King Priam begged for his son's body. Achilles wept with him, and gave Hector back.

panels.visual: The goddess Thetis dipping baby Achilles in the River Styx, holding him by one heel, glowing water
panels.caption: When Achilles was a baby, his mother dipped him in the River Styx. He became impossible to wound.

panels.visual: The baby Achilles held up, the water dripping, the heel dry with a tiny circle showing the dry spot
panels.caption: She held him by the heel, so the heel stayed dry. Later writers added this part: Homer never told it.

panels.visual: Paris the Trojan prince aiming a bow; Apollo's light guiding the arrow in a golden trail towards Achilles' heel
panels.caption: Apollo guided Paris's arrow into that one heel. Achilles died.

panels.visual: A modern doctor's diagram of the Achilles tendon at the back of the ankle with a label, Glauka wearing a stethoscope-like gag, pointing
panels.caption: We still call a weak spot an Achilles heel. The Achilles tendon takes its name from it.

panels.visual: King Aegeus (old, white beard, crown, purple cloak) stands on the Nike bastion of the Acropolis, hand on the shoulder of his young curly-haired son Theseus, both facing the harbour where a ship waits; sea behind
panels.caption: Aegeus sent his son Theseus to Crete to kill the Minotaur.
panels.narr: Hoo. Every nine years Athens had to send fourteen of its young people to Crete, to be fed to a monster, the Minotaur. This time the king's own son, Theseus, went to kill it.

panels.visual: Close-up of two hands clasped; Aegeus pointing to a folded white sail and a black sail lying side by side on the stone
panels.caption: The signal: white sails if Theseus lived. Black if he died.
panels.narr: The ship had black sails, because that is how you sail to a funeral. So the old king made a deal: white sails if Theseus lived, black if he died.

voice_speech.speaker: Aegeus
voice_speech.text: White sails, if you live. White sails. Promise me.

panels.visual: A black-sailed ship leaving the harbour under a heavy grey sky, tiny Theseus waving at the stern, small owl Glauka flying above
panels.caption: The ship sailed under black sails.
panels.narr: The ship sailed under black sails, and I flew with it to the headland. Everything rested on a teenage boy remembering something. You can guess where this is going.

panels.visual: King Aegeus alone at the edge of the cliff watching the horizon, wind in his white hair and purple cloak, Glauka perched on the wall beside him
panels.caption: Every day he climbed to the rock and watched the sea.
panels.narr: Then I came back to keep the old man company. Every day he climbed to this rock, the one under your feet, and watched the sea until dark.

voice_speech.speaker: Aegeus
voice_speech.text: Surely today. Surely, surely, white sails.

panels.visual: Theseus on the ship's deck, sword in hand, victorious and smiling, the Minotaur's horned head carved on a coin-like emblem in a thought bubble; behind him the Cretan coast fading
panels.caption: Theseus won in Crete. The ship turned for home.
panels.narr: Far away in Crete, Theseus killed the Minotaur and found his way out of the Labyrinth. The ship turned for home, and he was very pleased with himself.

panels.visual: The ship's crew hoisting sails; the sail being raised is BLACK; Theseus in the foreground with his hand on his forehead, staring at it in shock, tiny pupils, sweat drop
panels.caption: Theseus forgot.
panels.narr: So pleased that Theseus forgot. The crew hauled up the same black sails they had left with.

panels.visual: Dramatic wide view: the ship returning to Athens under black sails, golden sunset, tiny figure of Aegeus on the cliff top in silhouette
panels.caption: His ship came back under black sails.
panels.narr: His ship came back under black sails. From up here the sail is the first thing you see, long before faces, long before anyone can shout.

panels.visual: Close-up of Aegeus' face, huge eyes with a tiny black-sailed ship reflected in each pupil, a tear running into his white beard, radial speed lines
panels.caption: He believed his son was dead.
panels.narr: He believed his son was dead. (pause) Aegeus didn't wait to find out.

voice_speech.speaker: Aegeus
voice_speech.text: Black... black sails.

panels.visual: Aegeus seen from behind stepping to the edge of the high cliff, arms open, purple cloak billowing, the sea far below; no gore, dramatic manga angle
panels.caption: He threw himself from the rock.
panels.narr: He stepped off the rock.
panels.direction: Speak low, then silence. Let the SFX play.

panels.visual: Seabirds and a ring of white spray on the deep blue Aegean, the sea shown wide and calm, a purple cloak floating, soft light
panels.caption: The Aegean Sea is named after him.
panels.narr: When Theseus came ashore with his good news, the city was already weeping for its king. The sea kept the old man's name. We still call it the Aegean.

panels.visual: An old travel-writer (Pausanias, in a travelling hat with a scroll) points to the spot beside the little temple of Athena Nike, tourists looking
panels.caption: Pausanias was shown this spot beside the temple of Nike.
panels.narr: Was it really here? About eighteen hundred years ago a travel-writer called Pausanias climbed this hill. He wrote that this was the spot, beside the little Nike temple.

panels.visual: A split image: left half the Nike bastion in Athens, right half the cliffs of Cape Sounion with a temple, a big question mark between them, Glauka the owl shrugging a wing
panels.caption: Others said Cape Sounion. Nobody knows which is true.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: The story is old either way.

panels.narr: Guides at Cape Sounion, down the coast, say it was there. That's a myth: a story the Greeks told, not a thing that happened. But go to the edge and look south-west. That's his sea.

voice_speech.speaker: Glauka
voice_speech.text: Either way, the sails were black.

panels.visual: The bare rock of the Areopagus with the Acropolis behind it, a few stone steps carved into the rock, Glauka the owl on top
panels.caption: The Rock of Ares.
panels.narr: Hoo! This is the Rock of Ares, the god of war. The Greeks said the first murder trial in the world was held right here.

panels.visual: Ares the god of war (crested helmet, red cloak, fierce) standing over a fallen figure in the mist, a dark shape of a young man, no gore
panels.caption: Ares had killed a son of Poseidon.
panels.narr: Ares had killed a son of Poseidon. The young man, Halirrhothius, had attacked Ares's daughter, so Ares struck him down. Poseidon, the sea god, wanted his son's killer tried.

panels.visual: The twelve gods sitting on rough stone seats on the rock as judges, big robes and stern faces; Ares standing before them
panels.caption: The other gods sat on this stone, heard the case and judged him.
panels.narr: The other gods sat on this stone, heard the case and judged him. Twelve of them, on rough seats, with the god of war standing in the middle. They let him go.

panels.visual: A stone judge's gavel-like marble ballot and Glauka the owl whispering in a god's ear, the word FIRST in a banner
panels.caption: The first murder trial in the world.
panels.narr: The first murder trial in the world. I was there, on a god's shoulder. Maybe I whispered some advice. Nobody asked for it.

panels.visual: Young Orestes (dark curly hair, haggard, hunted look) stands before a jury of Athenians on the Areopagus rock; behind him dim shapes of the Furies with snakes in their hair
panels.caption: Much later, Orestes was tried on this same rock.
panels.narr: Much later, Orestes was tried on this same rock. Look behind him: the Furies, with snakes for hair. They hunt anyone who kills their own family. Now they had found him.

panels.visual: Orestes' face in an inset with a shadow of his mother Clytemnestra behind him
panels.caption: He had killed his own mother, Clytemnestra.
panels.narr: He had killed his own mother, Clytemnestra. She had murdered his father, King Agamemnon, so Orestes came home and killed her. Now the Furies wanted him dead.

panels.visual: A row of Athenian jurors dropping black and white pebbles into two urns, speed lines
panels.caption: The jury of Athenians voted.
panels.narr: The jury of Athenians voted. One by one they dropped their pebbles into the urns. Black for death. White for freedom.

panels.visual: Two equal piles of pebbles, the black and white heaps exactly the same height, jurors gasping with sweat drops
panels.caption: The votes came out exactly even.
panels.narr: Then they counted. Two piles. Exactly the same height. The votes came out exactly even: half for death, half for freedom.

panels.visual: Athena (helmet, spear, calm) stepping forward, placing a white pebble in the urn, golden light
panels.caption: Athena herself cast the deciding vote.
panels.narr: Athena had promised her vote to Orestes. She stepped forward. White.

voice_speech.speaker: Athena
voice_speech.text: My pebble is for Orestes.

panels.visual: Orestes sinking to his knees with relief, tears, the Furies fading into mist behind him
panels.caption: Orestes walked free.
panels.narr: Orestes walked free. He fell to his knees and cried. The Furies let him go, and Athena gave them a cave under this very rock. From then on, a tie set you free.

panels.visual: Saint Paul (an old traveller in a plain cloak, scroll in hand) speaking to a crowd on the rock in AD 51
panels.caption: In AD 51 Saint Paul stood here and spoke to the people of Athens.
panels.narr: That's a myth: a story the Greeks told, not a thing that happened. But this next part is real. In AD 51 Saint Paul stood here and spoke to the people of Athens.

panels.visual: A bronze plaque with Greek letters at the foot of the steps and Glauka reading it with a tiny scroll
panels.caption: His speech is cut into a bronze plaque.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: I have read it. I read Greek.

panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. The book of Acts in the Bible tells it, and the speech is cut into this bronze plaque. Find it, and mind the slippery rock.

panels.visual: Aristotle in fine clothes with rings on his fingers, thin legs, small eyes, lisping, a mirror in hand
panels.caption: Writers said Aristotle had thin legs and small eyes, a lisp, fine clothes and rings.

panels.visual: Aristotle cutting open a fish and a tiny octopus on a table, notebook and labelled sketches of hundreds of animals
panels.caption: He studied everything and described hundreds of animals.

panels.visual: A big pile of scrolls on stars, plants, poetry, politics and logic, with Aristotle perched at the top reading
panels.caption: Animals, plants, the stars, poetry, politics, how arguments work.

panels.visual: Aristotle writing in a book 'women have fewer teeth than men', his wife with a big smile showing a full set of teeth, comic
panels.caption: He thought women had fewer teeth than men. He never checked.

panels.visual: Aristotle (dandy, rings, fashionable hair) at Plato's Academy with a scroll, a bench of students, a clock showing twenty years
panels.caption: Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for about twenty years.

panels.visual: Aristotle tutoring a boy, the young Alexander the Great, with a map of the world
panels.caption: He tutored the young Alexander the Great.

panels.visual: Aristotle walking and talking under covered walkways of the Lyceum, a bunch of students struggling to keep up, out of breath
panels.caption: People say he taught while walking. His followers were called Peripatetics, the walkers-about.

panels.visual: Builders in 1996 digging a foundation and finding ancient ruins, an excited archaeologist, a modern crane behind
panels.caption: The ruins of the Lyceum were only found in 1996, when builders dug for a new museum.

panels.visual: Two little girls of about nine in white robes on the Acropolis near a small house with a view over the city
panels.caption: Every year two girls from noble families were chosen to live on the Acropolis for a year.

panels.visual: The girls helping weave a big saffron robe (the peplos) on a loom, threads and yarn balls, an old priestess watching
panels.caption: The girls helped start weaving the peplos, Athena's new robe.

panels.visual: The two girls at night with closed baskets balanced on their heads, descending a hidden stone passage lit by a tiny lamp
panels.caption: Once a year, at night, they carried closed baskets down a hidden passage.

panels.visual: The girls in a dark garden below the rock, exchanging baskets with a tiny puzzled expression, question marks
panels.caption: They did not know what was inside.

panels.visual: The sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus: marble temples among pines, sick people arriving on mules and carried on stretchers
panels.caption: Epidaurus was the most famous sanctuary of Asclepius, the god of healing.

panels.visual: A long hall with rows of beds where patients sleep, moonlight, a faint dream bubble of a robed god with a staff
panels.caption: They slept in a special hall, hoping the god would visit them in a dream.

panels.visual: Harmless little snakes slithering around the sanctuary floor, children leaning out in fear and wonder, Glauka watching
panels.caption: Harmless snakes slithered around the sanctuary.

panels.visual: A snake coiled round a staff, the symbol of medicine, and a stone tablet with writing: priests chiselling a list of cures
panels.caption: The snake on a staff is still the symbol of medicine. Stone tablets list the cures people claimed.

panels.visual: Wide view of the bare rock of the Acropolis in ancient times with a small village around it, Athena and Poseidon standing on opposite sides facing each other, sparks of rivalry between their eyes
panels.caption: Athena and Poseidon both wanted this city.
panels.narr: Hoo. Back then this rock was bare, with a few huts round the bottom. Athena and Poseidon both wanted this city. Look at them glaring.

panels.visual: Poseidon raising his trident high, muscles bulging, sea-green hair whipping
panels.caption: Poseidon struck the rock with his trident.
panels.narr: The rule was simple: give the people the best gift, and the city is yours. Poseidon went first, of course. He struck the rock with his trident.

panels.visual: The rock cracking open and a jet of water bursting upward in jagged white spray; astonished villagers
panels.caption: A spring gushed out.
panels.narr: A spring gushed out of solid rock, right up here on the dry hilltop. The villagers stared. Water from nowhere: what a gift.

voice_speech.speaker: Poseidon
voice_speech.text: Water! From a rock! Beat that.

panels.visual: An Athenian cupping the water and tasting it, tongue sticking out in disgust, comic sweat drop
panels.caption: The water was salty. Nobody could drink it.
panels.narr: Then somebody tasted it. The water was salty. He's the god of the sea: what did they expect? Nobody could drink it.

panels.visual: Athena kneeling calmly on the rock pressing a small olive sapling into the soil, owl Glauka on her shoulder
panels.caption: Athena planted an olive tree.
panels.narr: Athena didn't shout. She knelt down and planted an olive tree. I was sitting on her shoulder, so I saw it all.

voice_speech.speaker: Athena
voice_speech.text: I will. Quietly.

panels.visual: The olive sapling bursting into a full tree in golden light, leaves flying, villagers gazing up in awe
panels.caption: A gift.
panels.narr: The little tree shot up into a full olive tree, there and then. Olives to eat, oil for the lamps. A gift that comes back every single year.

panels.visual: A crowd of Athenian men and women raising their hands to vote, olive branches in hands, Poseidon sulking in the corner
panels.caption: The people chose the olive.
panels.narr: Then the whole village voted. Salt water you can't drink, or a tree that feeds you for ever? Up went the hands. The people chose the olive.

panels.visual: Athena, crested helmet pushed back, giving a small victorious smile; behind her the new city called Athens glows in light
panels.caption: The city was named for Athena.
panels.narr: So the city was named for Athena: Athens. She didn't cheer. Just a small smile, the way you smile when you knew all along.

panels.visual: Poseidon stomping away into the sea with waves rolling, grumbling expression, trident dragging
panels.caption: Poseidon lost the contest.
panels.narr: Poseidon lost the contest. He did not lose quietly: he stormed back into the sea and, in his rage, flooded the plain to the west.

panels.visual: Athena and her olive tree on the Acropolis, calm and regal, a temple rising in the background
panels.caption: She has been its goddess ever since.
panels.narr: Athena kept the city. She has been its goddess from that day to this, and later her temples went up on this very rock.

panels.visual: Close-up of marks in a rock floor, three trident-shaped holes, a hand pointing at them, an open roof above showing the sky
panels.caption: Under the north porch of the Erechtheion there are marks in the rock.
panels.narr: Now walk to the north porch of the Erechtheion. Under it there are marks in the rock. The Athenians told it like this: Poseidon's trident made them.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl peering at the trident marks with a monocle-like gleam
panels.caption: People said Poseidon's trident made them. The roof above was left open to the sky.
panels.narr: Above them, the roof was left open to the sky. That's a myth: a story the Greeks told, not a thing that happened. But the marks are real. Go and find them.

panels.visual: Two brothers, Atreus (dark beard, red cloak) and Thyestes (thinner, grey-streaked), glaring at each other across the throne of Mycenae, lightning between their eyes
panels.caption: Atreus and Thyestes hated each other. Both wanted to be king of Mycenae.
panels.narr: Two brothers, one throne. Atreus and Thyestes both wanted to be king of Mycenae. In the end Atreus won, and threw his brother out.

panels.visual: Close-up of Atreus smirking with one eyebrow raised, offering a hand in false friendship
panels.caption: Atreus pretended to make peace.
panels.narr: Then Atreus found out that Thyestes had stolen his wife as well. So Atreus pretended to make peace. He smiled. Never trust that smile.

voice_speech.speaker: Atreus
voice_speech.text: Brother! Come home. All is forgiven. Let us feast.

panels.visual: A long banquet hall with torches, a laden table, Thyestes hesitant at the door, servants hurrying
panels.caption: He invited Thyestes to a feast.
panels.narr: He invited Thyestes to a feast. Thyestes came home in rags and stood in the doorway a long time. Then he smelled the cooking, and came in.

panels.visual: A big pot of stew steaming, ladle, and Atreus' sinister shadow looming over it
panels.caption: He served him a stew.
panels.narr: Atreus served him a stew. He had cooked it himself, for his dear brother. That should have been the first clue.

panels.visual: Thyestes eating happily, spoon to his mouth, with a bowl of stew; Atreus watching with a wicked grin in the background
panels.caption: Thyestes ate.
panels.narr: Thyestes ate. Years on the road had made him hungry. He ate every spoonful, and Atreus watched every one.

panels.visual: Low dramatic angle across the table: Atreus lifts the lid off a silver platter towards Thyestes; we do NOT see what is on the platter: a white starburst of light and ink spikes hides it
panels.caption: More stew, brother?
panels.narr: Then the lid came off.

voice_speech.speaker: Atreus
voice_speech.text: More stew, brother?

panels.visual: Thyestes' face in the foreground frozen in horror, tiny pupils, sweat drops flying, silver spoon dropping
panels.caption: The stew was made from Thyestes' own sons.
panels.narr: On the platter were the heads and hands of Thyestes' sons. Now he knew what the stew was made from.

panels.visual: The sun in the sky above the Bronze Age citadel of Mycenae has a horrified manga face, hands on cheeks, its rays bending backwards; below, the rough boulder walls and the flat-roofed palace hall
panels.caption: The sun was so horrified that it turned back in the sky.
panels.narr: Even the sun couldn't watch. It was so horrified that it turned round in the sky, and went back the way it had come.

panels.visual: Thyestes on his feet, arm raised, pointing at Atreus with fury, his cloak swirling, black ink spikes
panels.caption: Thyestes cursed the whole family.
panels.narr: Thyestes had one weapon left. He cursed the family, every one of them.

voice_speech.speaker: Thyestes
voice_speech.text: A curse on your house! On your sons, and their sons!

panels.visual: A dark cloud of curse like a snake coiling over the Bronze Age palace citadel of Mycenae (rough boulder walls, flat-roofed palace hall) in a stormy sky
panels.caption: That curse did not stop with him.
panels.narr: That curse did not stop with him. Greek curses don't wear off. They wait, coiled over the palace like a snake.

panels.visual: A line of silhouettes of kings through the generations from father to son to son, each with a dark thread connecting them to the next
panels.caption: It ran down through the generations, from father to son to son.
panels.narr: It ran down through the generations, from father to son to son. Atreus had a son called Agamemnon. Keep an eye on that name. That curse is coming for him next.

panels.visual: The Lion Gate at night under a black sky with a faint red glow, Glauka watching from a tower
panels.caption: The house of Atreus was cursed.
panels.narr: The house of Atreus was cursed. That's a myth: a story the Greeks told, not a thing that happened. But the palace was real, up the hill. Climb and find it.

panels.visual: The great palace of Knossos with red columns and bright painted walls, Glauka the owl flying above
panels.caption: Knossos was the biggest palace of the Minoans, about three thousand five hundred years ago.

panels.visual: A bird's-eye view of a vast tangled maze of rooms, more than a thousand, a tiny lost visitor in the middle
panels.caption: More than a thousand rooms, all tangled together. People say this is where the Labyrinth story came from.

panels.visual: A Minoan wall painting in painted fresco style: a young man somersaulting over the back of a charging bull while a girl holds its horns
panels.caption: On the palace walls are paintings of young people who somersault over a charging bull.

panels.visual: A real bull charging in a courtyard with a trio of young acrobats in flight, dust and speed lines, the crowd cheering
panels.caption: Nobody knows if it was a sport, a ritual, or both. The bull was very real.

panels.visual: Six stone maidens (Caryatids) standing in a row as columns of the Erechtheion porch, baskets on their heads supporting the roof, golden light
panels.caption: Six of us hold up the roof of this porch on our heads.
panels.narr: Six of us once held up the roof of this porch, on our heads. No hands. Count the places: four in front, two behind.

panels.visual: Close-up: one Caryatid's carved face slowly opening her eyes, a faint smile, tiny dust falling from her stone lashes
panels.caption: I am a Caryatid.
panels.narr: Yes, the stone is talking. You have to stand very still to hear us. Most people never do.

voice_speech.speaker: Caryatid
voice_speech.text: I am a Caryatid. One of six sisters.

panels.visual: Seen from below, a Caryatid's head and the stone roof resting on it, birds nesting nearby, centuries passing as clock-hands
panels.caption: We have stood here a very long time.
panels.narr: We stood up there for more than two thousand years. Armies came and went. Birds nested on our heads. We held the roof.

panels.visual: Wide shot of tourists and school groups walking under the porch, taking photographs
panels.caption: Everyone looks up at us.
panels.narr: Everyone looks up at us: crowds of faces, little clicking boxes. Nobody asks what we are carrying, or for how long.

panels.visual: Five modern concrete-grey copies of the Caryatids standing on the porch with a sign in the shadow, Glauka pointing at one
panels.caption: The maidens you see outside are copies.
panels.narr: Here's a secret: the maidens you see out here are copies, every one of them. The real sisters moved indoors, down the hill.

panels.visual: Inside the Acropolis Museum: five original Caryatids glowing in a bright hall, protected behind glass, calm
panels.caption: Five of the originals are in the Acropolis Museum, safe from the weather.
panels.narr: Five of us are in the Acropolis Museum now, safe from the weather. Warm, dry, well lit. We hold up nothing at all.

panels.visual: Caryatid close-up shrugging with a stone shrug and a tiny weary eyebrow raised
panels.caption: I do not mind. Much.
panels.narr: Do I miss the porch? The sky, the wind, the roof on my head?

voice_speech.speaker: Caryatid
voice_speech.text: I do not mind. Much.

panels.visual: A small group of the Caryatid sisters in the Museum looking sideways with a gentle, grumpy expression
panels.caption: The sisters keep each other company.
panels.narr: Down here, the five of us keep each other company. But look closely at our row. There is a space where a sister should be.

panels.visual: Lord Elgin's men (nineteenth-century Englishmen in tall hats and coats) hauling a statue on ropes and wooden rollers, Greek workers watching
panels.caption: The sixth sister was taken to London by Lord Elgin's men around 1801.
panels.narr: The sixth sister was taken by Lord Elgin's men, around 1801. Ropes, rollers, then a ship to London. Nobody asked her.

panels.visual: A statue of a Caryatid in a grand museum in London with tall windows and foggy weather outside
panels.caption: She is still there.
panels.narr: She is still there.

panels.visual: The empty gap among the Caryatids: five in a row and a dark space where the sixth should stand, a gentle sad atmosphere
panels.caption: Her place on the porch is empty.
panels.narr: Up on the porch, a copy stands in her place now. But down in the museum, beside the five of us, her place is still empty.

panels.visual: The Caryatid sisters in a row, all looking in the same direction, towards the west, with a tear-like drop of rain on one stone cheek
panels.caption: We have been waiting a long time.
panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and you can visit her in the British Museum today. Now go down to the Acropolis Museum and find the gap where she should stand.

voice_speech.speaker: Caryatid
voice_speech.text: We have been waiting. We can wait longer.

panels.visual: King Agamemnon (dark hair, short beard, red cloak, bronze armour) riding home in a chariot to Mycenae with treasure carts behind him, crowds cheering
panels.caption: Ten years later Agamemnon came home from Troy, victorious and rich.
panels.narr: Agamemnon came home to Mycenae after ten years at war in Troy. He rode in a chariot, with carts full of treasure behind him. The crowds cheered. Almost everyone did.

panels.visual: Clytemnestra in the palace doorway watching in stern silence, her fists tightly clenched, a flash of anger in her eyes
panels.caption: His wife Clytemnestra had never forgiven him for Iphigenia.
panels.narr: His wife Clytemnestra did not cheer. She had never forgiven him for Iphigenia, the daughter he sacrificed so that his ships could sail.

panels.visual: A small inset memory of a white-veiled girl, Iphigenia, at an altar, in a soft ghostly frame
panels.caption: She had been waiting a long time.
panels.narr: That's Iphigenia, at the altar. Her mother had waited ten years for this day. Ten years is a long time to stay angry.

panels.visual: Clytemnestra welcoming Agamemnon with a perfect false smile, red carpet beneath his feet, cold eyes
panels.narr: She laid a red carpet from his chariot to the door. That was a welcome for a god, not a man. He walked on it anyway.

voice_speech.speaker: Clytemnestra
voice_speech.text: Welcome home, husband. Your bath is ready.

panels.visual: Mycenae palace bath chamber: steam, a bath, Agamemnon rising from it
panels.caption: As he stepped out of his bath.
panels.narr: Ten years at war. All he wanted was a hot bath. Fair enough. He stood up to step out.

panels.visual: A heavy net thrown over King Agamemnon, his silhouette struggling under it, Clytemnestra in silhouette with blazing red eyes, an axe raised against a red burst, no wound shown
panels.caption: She threw a net over him.
panels.narr: She threw a net over him, so he could not move. Then the axe.

panels.visual: The palace corridor with a red glow under the door, servants frozen in fear, silent
panels.caption: The bath.
panels.narr: Out in the corridor, the servants heard everything through the door. Nobody went in. Not one of them said a word.

panels.visual: Clytemnestra's face lit from below in red, determined, the axe's shadow on the wall
panels.caption: She had waited ten years.
panels.narr: She had waited ten years. Now the king of Mycenae was dead, killed by his own wife, in his own bath.

panels.visual: Young Orestes (a teenager with dark curly hair, travelling cloak) returning to Mycenae in a dust-storm, a grim hand on a sword
panels.caption: Years later their son Orestes came back.
panels.narr: But the curse on this family was not finished. Years later their son Orestes came back, with a sword.

panels.visual: Orestes standing over his mother with his sword lowered, her stern face, deep shadows, no blow shown
panels.caption: He killed his mother to avenge his father.
panels.narr: He killed his mother to avenge his father. In this family that is how the curse works: every killing asks for another.

panels.visual: Three Furies (winged women with snakes in their hair and red eyes) chasing Orestes across a stormy landscape
panels.caption: Then the Furies hunted him across the world.
panels.narr: Then the Furies came for him: women with snakes in their hair, who hunt anyone who kills their own family. They chased him across the world.

panels.visual: Athena standing in white light on the Areopagus rock with a pebble raised and Orestes kneeling in front of her, relieved
panels.caption: Athena herself cast the deciding vote and set him free.
panels.narr: On the Areopagus, Athena herself cast the deciding vote and set him free. That's a myth: a story the Greeks told, not a thing that happened. But that rock is real. Climb it.

panels.visual: The enormous stone walls of Mycenae in the sun, huge irregular boulders fitted together, tiny people at the bottom for scale
panels.caption: Look at the walls of Mycenae.
panels.narr: Look at the walls of Mycenae. See the little people at the bottom? Now look how far the stones go up above their heads.

panels.visual: Close-up of a boulder with a person's hand beside it for scale, stone texture, a sweat drop
panels.caption: Some of the boulders weigh several tonnes.
panels.narr: Some of these boulders weigh several tonnes, about as much as an elephant. Put your hand on one and push. Go on. Nothing.

panels.visual: Later Greeks (in tunics) staring up at the walls with their mouths open, pointing, cartoon amazement
panels.caption: Later Greeks decided no ordinary person could have lifted them.
panels.narr: Hundreds of years later, Greeks came up this hill and stared. No ordinary person, they decided, could have lifted stones like these.

panels.visual: A one-eyed giant Cyclops with a big amber eye straining with a boulder on his shoulders, in a legendary glow
panels.caption: They said only the Cyclopes could have done it.
panels.narr: So they said only the Cyclopes could have done it: giants with one round eye in the middle of the forehead, and shoulders like hills.

panels.visual: Extreme low angle: a Cyclops slams a gigantic boulder into the wall, chips of stone flying, amber eye glaring
panels.caption: The one-eyed giants.
panels.narr: The one-eyed giants. In the story, a Cyclops could slam a boulder into the wall with one shove. A travel-writer called Pausanias wrote it down.

panels.visual: Several Cyclopes working at the walls, one stacking, one chiselling, one eating a sandwich-sized loaf of bread
panels.caption: The name stuck.
panels.narr: The name stuck. People told the story so often that everybody pictured giants on the building site. Look at that one with the loaf. Even giants stop for lunch.

panels.visual: An archaeologist with a notebook and a hat looking at the wall, a thought bubble of a Cyclops being crossed out
panels.caption: Archaeologists still call this kind of building Cyclopean.
panels.narr: Archaeologists still call this kind of building Cyclopean. They use the giants' name every day, but they don't believe in the giants.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl perched on a boulder with a smug expression and one wing raised
panels.caption: Even though they know exactly who built it.
panels.narr: Even though they know exactly who built it. Want to meet the builders? Turn the page.

panels.visual: Real Mycenaean workers (men in simple tunics) hauling a huge stone up a sloping ramp with ropes, leaning, sweating
panels.caption: Real people built these walls about 3,300 years ago.
panels.narr: Real people built these walls, about 3,300 years ago. Look at the men in front, leaning hard into the ropes.

panels.visual: A long wooden lever under a boulder, workers pushing down, the boulder lifting
panels.caption: They used ramps and levers.
panels.narr: They used ramps to drag the stones uphill, and long wooden levers to tip them into place. Three men on one pole. Push, push. There.

panels.visual: A line of workers with ropes and sleds dragging a stone across the ground, dusty, a foreman shouting
panels.caption: And a great deal of muscle.
panels.narr: And a great deal of muscle. A whole team on the ropes, one man shouting at all of them. Slowly, the stone moves.

panels.visual: The finished walls at sunset with a tiny Cyclops silhouette fading into a tiny winking sun, Glauka looking on
panels.caption: No giants were involved.
panels.narr: No giants were involved. That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. The walls are still here. You can put your hand on them.

panels.visual: Diogenes lying in a huge clay jar (pithos) in the Agora, a cloak, a stick and a bag beside him, a scruffy dog at his feet
panels.caption: Diogenes lived in a big clay jar. He owned a cloak, a stick and a bag.

panels.visual: A boy scooping water in his cupped hands from a fountain and drinking, Diogenes watching
panels.caption: One day he saw a boy scoop up water in his hands and drink.

speech.speaker: Diogenes
speech.text: Even my cup is too much.

panels.visual: Alexander the Great (young, golden armour and a purple cape) standing over Diogenes' jar with soldiers behind him, the sun behind him
panels.caption: Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted.

speech.speaker: Diogenes
speech.text: Stand a little out of my sunlight.

panels.visual: Diogenes' dog barking at a crowd while Diogenes grins and begs in the street, a comic scene
panels.caption: People called him the dog. His followers were Cynics, from the Greek for dog-like.

panels.visual: Diogenes walking through the busy Agora in broad daylight holding a lit lamp, shopkeepers staring
panels.caption: Diogenes walked through the Agora in broad daylight carrying a lit lamp.

panels.visual: Diogenes peering with his lamp into the face of a puzzled Athenian merchant, big eyes
panels.caption: He held the lamp up to every face.

panels.visual: Plato at the board of his school drawing a two-legged stick figure 'a featherless biped', students nodding
panels.caption: Plato described a human being as a featherless biped.

panels.visual: Diogenes holding up a plucked chicken in front of Plato's school, students laughing, Plato shocked
panels.caption: Diogenes held up a plucked chicken outside Plato's school.

panels.visual: A sunny garden outside Athens: Epicurus (gentle, curly beard, simple clothes) with Leontion writing a scroll and the young slave Mys studying, men and women learning together under fig trees; a small sign on the garden gate reads STRANGER, YOU WILL DO WELL TO STAY HERE
panels.caption: Around 306 BC Epicurus bought a garden and taught there. Men, women, even slaves.

panels.visual: A simple table with a loaf of bread, a jug of water and a tiny pot of cheese, Epicurus beaming with delight, a letter beside it
panels.caption: Bread and water make me happy. Send me a little pot of cheese, so that I can have a feast.

panels.visual: Atoms swirling and scattering in a cosmic swirl at the top; below on clouds, the gods lounging bored and uninterested, one yawning, one eating grapes, ignoring the world
panels.caption: Do not fear the gods: they do not meddle with us. Everything is made of tiny atoms.

panels.visual: Epicurus calm with a gentle smile, atoms drifting like dust in a sunbeam, a ribbon with the quote
panels.caption: Do not fear death. When we die, the atoms simply scatter.

speech.speaker: Epicurus
speech.text: Where death is, I am not.

panels.visual: The Agora: rivals whispering behind their hands, pointing at the Garden; in a small inset a Stoic writing and forging rude letters by candlelight with a mean smirk, a pile of fifty letters
panels.caption: Enemies hated that women and slaves were welcome. They spread rumours, and a rival Stoic forged fifty rude letters in his name.

panels.visual: Split image: on the left a cartoon of a huge fat 'Epicurus the glutton' stuffing his face at a banquet, on the right the real Epicurus quietly eating a piece of bread with a cup of water; a bold line between them
panels.caption: They said he overate till he was sick. He lived on bread and water.

panels.visual: A big open dictionary page with the word EPICURE highlighted and a big red stamp reading UNFAIR!, Glauka the owl pointing indignantly at it
panels.caption: The insult stuck: today an epicure means someone who loves rich food.

panels.visual: Old Epicurus sitting in the garden surrounded by his smiling friends, Leontion, Mys and others, warm golden light, his eyes crinkled with a peaceful smile despite a blanket round his legs
panels.caption: He died in 270 BC in great pain, writing to a friend that remembering their conversations made it a happy day.

panels.visual: Wide sunlit view of the ancient theatre at Epidaurus: perfectly curved stone rows rising up a green hillside, pine trees, a circular stage
panels.caption: Built around 340 BC.
panels.narr: Hoo! Welcome to Epidaurus. Sick people came to this valley to ask the god Asclepius to heal them. This theatre was built here around 340 BC.

panels.visual: A full crowd of 14,000 spectators sitting on the rows, tiny dots for faces
panels.caption: It seats about 14,000 people.
panels.narr: It seats about 14,000 people. Fill every seat. Now imagine you're in the very last row, and one man down there starts to speak.

panels.visual: A modern performance in the same theatre: actors in masks on the circular stage, evening lights
panels.caption: It is still used for plays today.
panels.narr: It is still used for plays today. Actors stand in that same circle. The whole hillside listens.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl flying over the rows with a proud expression
panels.caption: Its acoustics are famous.
panels.narr: Its acoustics are famous. That's the grown-up word for how sound travels in a place like this.

panels.visual: An actor at the centre circle speaking in a normal calm voice, small sound-wave rings spreading out
panels.caption: An actor speaking in a normal voice at the centre...
panels.narr: Here's the test. An actor stands in the centre and speaks in a normal voice. No shouting, no microphone.

panels.visual: The very top row, tiny spectators leaning forward and hearing him perfectly, wavy sound lines reaching them
panels.caption: ...can be heard in the top rows, without any microphone.
panels.narr: And right up in the top rows, the people at the very back can hear him. Every word.

panels.visual: A coin dropping on the stage with a tiny 'tink' sound-effect and a hand cupped behind an ear at the top
panels.caption: Guides say you can hear a coin drop or a match struck.
panels.narr: Guides go further. They say you can hear a coin drop, or a match struck, from the very top. Listen.

panels.visual: Glauka at the top of the rows hand-to-ear-feather, eyes closed with a little smile
panels.caption: Try it and see.
panels.narr: Is that true, or just a guide's favourite story? Don't take anyone's word for it. Not even mine. Try it and see.

panels.visual: Scientists in a diagram-like drawing: sound waves coming from the stage, bouncing off the stone steps, rows of seats drawn as a ribbed surface
panels.caption: Scientists think the rows of seats filter out the low background noise.
panels.narr: Modern scientists, not those two in robes, think the rows of seats filter out the low background noise.

panels.visual: Low rumbles of background noise shown as grey wavy lines being stopped by the rows of stone
panels.caption: The low noise is filtered away.
panels.narr: Wind in the pines, shuffling feet, somebody's tummy rumbling: the low noises hit the stone steps and get filtered away.

panels.visual: The voice shown as crisp bright lines passing through the stone steps, clean and clear
panels.caption: So the voice comes through clean.
panels.narr: So the voice comes through clean, like a bright thread pulled all the way up to the top row.

panels.visual: Glauka tapping a stone seat with one claw, a small ring of sound
panels.caption: The stone does some of the work.
panels.narr: The stone does some of the work. That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. You can test it today, with one coin and one sister.

panels.visual: The Parthenon as a mosque with a minaret, Ottoman guards on the Acropolis walls, calm blue sky, Glauka on a column
panels.caption: It was a temple, then a church, then a mosque.
panels.narr: Hoo. I've sat on these columns a very long time. In my day this was a temple. Later it was a church, then a mosque, with a minaret on the side.

panels.visual: The building complete under its roof across the centuries, three small inset pictures: a temple with a golden statue, a church with a cross, a mosque with a crescent
panels.caption: For two thousand years the Parthenon kept its roof.
panels.narr: Gods changed. Prayers changed. The building didn't. For two thousand years the Parthenon stood almost whole, roof and all.

panels.visual: Venetian ships and an army camp under General Morosini at the foot of the Acropolis, cannons smoking, banners with winged lions
panels.caption: In 1687 a Venetian army under Morosini besieged the Acropolis.
panels.narr: Then, in 1687, a Venetian army under General Morosini besieged the Acropolis: they surrounded it and attacked. Ottoman Turks held the top. The Venetians wanted it.

panels.visual: Inside the Parthenon, Ottoman soldiers stacking barrels of gunpowder under the old roof, a sweat drop
panels.caption: The Ottomans stored gunpowder inside the Parthenon.
panels.narr: Ottoman soldiers needed a strong place for their gunpowder, so they stored it inside the Parthenon, barrel after barrel. One spark was all it would take.

panels.visual: A big mortar firing from a hill, a flaming shell in the air over Athens, long curved speed lines
panels.caption: Morosini's guns fired on the Acropolis.
panels.narr: Morosini's guns fired on the Acropolis. Shell after shell went up, and came down on rock and wall. Then one came down somewhere else.

panels.visual: Close-up of a mortar shell dropping through a hole in the roof of the Parthenon, the barrels of gunpowder below, tiny white dots of fear
panels.caption: A mortar shell came through the roof.
panels.narr: A mortar shell came through the roof. Straight down, into the room full of barrels.

panels.visual: Black silhouette of the Parthenon with the middle blowing apart in white-hot light, columns flying, smoke; shown wide and vivid
panels.caption: 26 September 1687.
panels.narr: The twenty-sixth of September, 1687.
panels.direction: Say the date, then silence for the DOOOM.

panels.visual: Smoke clearing over the half-ruined Parthenon: broken columns in rubble, a tiny Glauka looking down
panels.caption: About three hundred people died.
panels.narr: (pause) When the smoke cleared, the middle of the Parthenon was gone. About three hundred people died.

panels.visual: The ruined Parthenon at dawn, with empty spaces where the middle was, Glauka perched on a broken column
panels.caption: It is a ruin because of an explosion, not old age.
panels.narr: In the morning I came back to my column. Two thousand years of standing, undone by one shell. It is a ruin because of an explosion, not old age.

panels.visual: A big close-up of the broken column drums scattered, hand-drawn arrows showing the missing middle
panels.caption: The middle of the building blew apart.
panels.narr: Look where the arrows point. The middle of the building blew apart, and columns from both long sides came down in pieces.

panels.visual: Modern tourists with cameras climbing the Acropolis steps with a tiny girl-and-owl pointing up
panels.caption: Today we visit what is left.
panels.narr: Today we visit what is left. Crowds climb these steps every day to see a building that was blown up, not worn down.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl flying right at us with a cute stern face, caption box beside her
panels.caption: Remember: an explosion, not time.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: Gunpowder stored in a temple, always a bad idea.

panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and the proof is the gap in the middle of each long side. An explosion, not time. Go and find it.

panels.visual: The Acropolis in April 1941 with a huge dark-red occupation banner (no symbols) hanging from the flagpole above the temples, grey-uniformed soldiers small in the distance, a sad dark sky, Glauka in the corner
panels.caption: In April 1941 the German army took Athens. They raised their banner on the Acropolis.

panels.visual: Two Greek students (young men in dark jackets) creeping up the rock at night under the moon, tiptoeing
panels.caption: On the night of 30 May 1941 two students climbed up.

panels.visual: The two students tearing the banner down from its pole at night, flag falling like a cloth, hearts racing
panels.caption: Manolis Glezos and Apostolos Santas tore the flag down and took it away.

panels.visual: A young Greek guard wrapped in the Greek flag on the rock edge in a hazy memory-like dotted frame with a question mark
panels.caption: A story says a young guard, Konstantinos Koukidis, wrapped himself in the flag and jumped. Historians are not sure it happened.

panels.visual: A grand wedding feast in a marble hall: guests in tunics at long tables turn to the doorway, where Eris, goddess of strife (wild black hair, dark ragged cloak, sly grin), tosses a shining golden apple across the floor
panels.caption: Eris, goddess of strife, was not invited to the wedding.
panels.narr: Eris, goddess of strife, was not invited to the wedding.

voice_speech.speaker: Eris
voice_speech.text: I brought a present.

panels.visual: Close-up of the golden apple rolling on the marble floor, a Greek-style inscription band on it, startled feet around, speed lines
panels.caption: She rolled in a golden apple: 'For the fairest.'
panels.narr: She rolled in a golden apple: 'For the fairest.'

panels.visual: Three goddesses all grabbing for the golden apple at once: Hera (regal, purple gown, diadem), Athena (crested helmet, spear, white chiton), Aphrodite (flowing pink gown, long golden hair), manga rivalry faces with sparks between their eyes
panels.caption: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed it.
panels.narr: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed it.

voice_speech.speaker: Aphrodite
voice_speech.text: Obviously mine.

panels.visual: Zeus on his throne, thunderbolt on his knee, holds both hands up refusing, sweating; Hermes (winged hat, winged sandals, caduceus) beside him pointing out of the hall, the three goddesses glaring in the background
panels.caption: Zeus would not choose between them.
panels.narr: Zeus would not choose between them.

voice_speech.speaker: Zeus
voice_speech.text: Not me. Ask him.

panels.visual: Mount Ida in the sun: Hermes leads the three goddesses up a rocky path, and Paris, a handsome young shepherd-prince in a red Phrygian cap with a crook, sheep around him, looks up bewildered
panels.caption: Hermes led them to Paris, a shepherd-prince on Mount Ida.
panels.narr: Hermes led them to Paris, a shepherd-prince on Mount Ida.

voice_speech.speaker: Paris
voice_speech.text: Me?

panels.visual: Paris in the middle looking dizzy while the three goddesses lean in, each making her pitch: Hera holds out a gold crown of tiny cities, Athena stands before a vision of armies and a victory wreath, Aphrodite whispers, a dreamy thought bubble behind her of a beautiful woman (Helen)
panels.caption: Hera offered power. Athena offered victory. Aphrodite offered Helen.

speech.speaker: Aphrodite
speech.text: The most beautiful woman in the world.

panels.narr: Hera offered power. Athena offered victory. Aphrodite offered Helen.

voice_speech.speaker: Aphrodite
voice_speech.text: The most beautiful woman in the world.

panels.visual: Paris smiling nervously handing the golden apple to a delighted Aphrodite, while Hera and Athena behind them are furious, steaming, fists clenched, dark storm clouds
panels.caption: Paris chose Aphrodite.
panels.narr: Paris chose Aphrodite.

voice_speech.speaker: Paris
voice_speech.text: Sorry, you two.

panels.visual: Glauka the little owl perched on a rock on the south slope of the Acropolis, the golden apple beside her, a huge ghostly Athena glowering from a cloud above, a tiny fleet of ships far on the sea behind
panels.caption: That's a myth. Helen was already married, and Athena never forgave him.
panels.narr: That's a myth. Helen was already married, and Athena never forgave him.

panels.visual: The great city of Alexandria in Egypt with the lighthouse and the library, a clear banner reading ALEXANDRIA, EGYPT
panels.caption: Hypatia lived and taught in Alexandria, in Egypt. Not in Athens.

panels.visual: Hypatia lecturing with an astrolabe and scrolls to an attentive crowd of students from far away
panels.caption: Around AD 400 she taught mathematics, astronomy and Plato's philosophy.

panels.visual: Hypatia driving her own chariot through Alexandria's busy street, people watching with admiration and tension
panels.caption: She drove her own chariot and lectured in public.

panels.visual: A quiet, sad panel: an astrolabe and a few broken pottery shards (ostraka) lying on a church floor, a dark crowd's silhouettes at the edge of the frame; no violence shown
panels.caption: In AD 415 she was killed by a mob. A Christian historian condemned it.

panels.visual: Daedalus (an elderly inventor with a beard) locked in a stone tower with his son Icarus, Glauka on the window sill
panels.caption: King Minos locked Daedalus in a tower with his son Icarus.

panels.visual: Daedalus stitching feathers with thread and wax into huge wings, the boy trying them on
panels.caption: Daedalus made two pairs of wings from feathers, thread and wax.

panels.visual: Daedalus warning Icarus with a finger, a diagram of a path between the sea spray and the sun
panels.caption: Not too low. Not too high. Fly the middle path.

panels.visual: Icarus soaring too near the sun laughing, wax running like tears, feathers loosening, a small figure falling toward a blue sea far below; no gore
panels.caption: Icarus forgot the middle path. That sea is still called the Icarian Sea.

panels.visual: A Greek fleet at Aulis with motionless ships on a flat calm sea, limp sails, soldiers sweating
panels.caption: The ships were stuck at Aulis with no wind at all. Agamemnon had angered Artemis.

panels.visual: A seer in a hooded cloak whispering to King Agamemnon who is turning pale, a flash of cold
panels.caption: A seer told him the wind would come only if he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia.

panels.visual: King Agamemnon's face, torn between duty and grief, a tear running into his black beard, red cloak; behind him Iphigenia in a white veil with bowed head before an altar; no knife, no blood
panels.caption: No wind.

panels.visual: A white deer leaping through speed lines at the altar while a soft light carries Iphigenia away in the clouds, the sails of the ships filling with wind
panels.caption: In some versions, Artemis swapped her for a deer. The wind blew, and the ships sailed for Troy.

panels.visual: The harbour town of Nafplio in the 1830s with a fortress above, flags, the new Greek capital looking busy
panels.caption: Nafplio was the first capital of modern Greece after independence.

panels.visual: Ioannis Kapodistrias (dignified man in a dark coat, white hair) walking up the street to church with guards behind
panels.caption: Its first head of state was Ioannis Kapodistrias.

panels.visual: The church of Saint Spyridon in Nafplio on a dawn street, a quiet moment before danger, two shadows lurking at the corner
panels.caption: On 9 October 1831 he was attacked outside the church of Saint Spyridon by two men from a rival family.

panels.visual: A small bullet hole in the church wall behind a pane of glass, a hand pointing at it, Glauka perched beside it
panels.caption: A bullet hole is still in the wall, behind glass, for nearly two hundred years.

panels.visual: Ariadne in the maze-like palace corridors, young, clever, holding a ball of red thread, Daedalus the inventor in the background
panels.caption: Daedalus built the Labyrinth so cleverly that once inside you could not find the way out.

panels.visual: Ariadne handing Theseus a ball of red thread at the door of the Labyrinth, whispering
panels.caption: Ariadne loved Theseus, and gave him a ball of thread.

speech.speaker: Ariadne
speech.text: Tie the end at the door.

panels.visual: Theseus walking into the dark winding corridors, red thread unrolling behind him through the dark, torch in hand
panels.caption: He tied the end at the door and let it unroll as he walked deeper in.

panels.visual: A bird's-eye view of a maze with a single red line winding through it, a tiny hero at the centre
panels.caption: Not even Daedalus was sure he could find the way out.

panels.visual: Deep in the dark Labyrinth: the Minotaur, a massive bull-headed giant with bloodshot glowing eyes, flared steaming nostrils, nose ring, looms out of the blackness; in the foreground Theseus seen from behind, sword in hand, a red thread trailing
panels.caption: Follow the thread.

panels.visual: The Minotaur charging at Theseus, speed lines, stone walls cracking, Theseus ready with a sword, dust cloud hiding the clash; no gore
panels.caption: He found the Minotaur in the dark and killed it.

panels.visual: Two small inset pictures side by side: Theseus with his bare hands, and Theseus with a sword; a big question mark between them
panels.caption: With his bare hands, or with a sword. The stories disagree.

panels.visual: Theseus following the red thread back out of the Labyrinth to a bright doorway, Ariadne waiting with open arms in the light
panels.caption: Then he followed the thread back out to the light.

panels.visual: The Lion Gate of Mycenae at golden hour, two stone lions facing each other on either side of a central column above a massive doorway
panels.caption: The main gate of Mycenae, built around 1250 BC.
panels.narr: About eighteen hundred years ago, a travel-writer called Pausanias climbed this road and stopped right here. The main gate of Mycenae, built around 1250 BC. Even then it was old.

panels.visual: Two stone lions, close-up of their bodies and paws on the altar, a column between them, rays of light
panels.caption: Two lions stand either side of a column, carved in stone.
panels.narr: He looked up, the way you're about to. Two lions stand either side of a column, carved in stone, their front paws up on a stone base.

panels.visual: A map of Europe sculpted history shown as a stone with the date 1250 BC and Glauka pointing at a scroll
panels.caption: The oldest large sculpture still standing in Europe.
panels.narr: Pausanias wrote that lions stand over the gate. They still do. It's the oldest large sculpture still standing in Europe. Older than me. I don't say that often.

panels.visual: Chiefs and chariots passing through the great gate in ancient times, banners, fierce soldiers in bronze
panels.caption: Chariots rolled through it.
panels.narr: Chariots rolled through it, horses first, soldiers running alongside. Whoever came home to Mycenae came home under these lions.

panels.visual: The lions' necks with the heads missing, empty round sockets, a sad but cute Glauka looking at the gap
panels.caption: The lions' heads were made separately and fitted on.
panels.narr: Now look closer at the lions. Something's wrong. Their heads were made separately and fitted on. Look at those empty holes.

panels.visual: Lost heads: two lion heads in a dream cloud drifting away over the centuries, cartoon-like
panels.caption: They are gone now, lost somewhere in the centuries.
panels.narr: They are gone now, lost somewhere in the centuries. Knocked off? Carried away? Buried under the rubble? Nobody has ever found them.

panels.visual: A tourist-view photo style panel: the lion bodies and the empty space, a question mark above the gap
panels.caption: What you see is the bodies and the empty space.
panels.narr: So what you see is the bodies, and an empty space at the top, where the faces should be glaring down at you.

panels.visual: Glauka drawing in the air what the heads would look like, with a dotted outline of lion heads
panels.caption: Where the heads should be.
panels.narr: Where the heads should be. Close your eyes and put them back. Bigger. No, bigger than that.

panels.visual: A worn stone threshold, deep grooves where the doors swung, a close-up shot with a hand tracing them
panels.caption: Look down at the threshold.
panels.narr: Now look down at the threshold, the big stone under your feet. Run your hand along it. Feel the grooves?

panels.visual: Great wooden doors swinging open on grooves in the stone, dust flying
panels.caption: The grooves show where the great doors swung open.
panels.narr: The grooves show where the great doors swung open and shut, again and again, for years and years.

panels.visual: Chariot wheels rolling over the stone threshold, tracks left in the stone, speed lines
panels.caption: And where chariot wheels rolled through.
panels.narr: And where chariot wheels rolled through. Right here. Under the lions. Over this stone.

panels.visual: Present-day: two little visitors' feet on the threshold stone fitting the grooves, Glauka perched on the gate above them
panels.caption: You stand where they stood.
panels.narr: You stand where they stood. That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. The grooves are under your feet. Now look up at the lions, and picture their heads.

panels.visual: Spartans carrying huge heavy iron bars as money, a wagon creaking under a pile of iron bars for a single purchase, a rich man sweating; Lycurgus (stern, dignified, from the sheet) overseeing with arms folded
panels.caption: Lycurgus is said to have given Sparta its laws, with money made of heavy iron bars so that nobody could get rich.

panels.visual: A split panel: left, a furious rich young man striking Lycurgus with a stick, Lycurgus clutching a hand over his eye (no blood); right, Lycurgus kindly leading the young man into his house, the young man bowing
panels.caption: A young man knocked out Lycurgus's eye. Lycurgus took him in, and he became his most loyal follower.

panels.visual: A crowd of Spartans raising their hands to swear an oath, and Lycurgus (one eye covered with a patch) walking away alone up a road toward Delphi at sunset, never looking back
panels.caption: He made the Spartans swear to keep his laws until he came back. He went to Delphi and never returned.

panels.visual: A different man, the Athenian Lycurgus (a statesman in 330 BC), supervising workers laying stone seats in the Theatre of Dionysus, and scribes copying scrolls of plays at a table; a big 'TWO MEN' sign with two different faces
panels.caption: Athens had its own Lycurgus, a real one, about 330 BC. He rebuilt the theatre in stone and had official copies made of the plays. Don't mix them up.

panels.visual: Heinrich Schliemann (Victorian archaeologist with a moustache, hat and spade) in a royal grave pit at Mycenae holding a golden mask up to the sun
panels.caption: In 1876 Schliemann dug up royal graves at Mycenae, full of gold.

panels.visual: A beaten gold face mask with big eyes and a moustache, shining on a velvet cloth, rays of light
panels.caption: Among the gold were face masks beaten from thin sheets of metal.

panels.visual: Schliemann pointing dramatically at the mask with a big speech bubble, comic pose
panels.caption: He is often quoted as saying, I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon.

speech.speaker: Schliemann
speech.text: I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon!

panels.visual: A timeline: the mask, labelled 300 years older than any Trojan War, a big red 'NOT AGAMEMNON' stamp, Glauka shaking her head
panels.caption: The mask is about 300 years older than any Trojan War could have been. Perhaps he never said the famous sentence.

panels.visual: A young Theseus lifting a huge heavy rock to take the sword and sandals hidden under it, muscles straining, an old palace on the Acropolis behind, a hill-top
panels.caption: Aegeus had left a sword and a pair of sandals under a heavy rock.
panels.narr: Far from Athens, a boy heaves up a rock his father left for him. Under it: a sword, sandals, and an order. Come to Athens.

panels.visual: Theseus setting off along a dusty road to Athens, sword on his hip, defeating a lurking bandit in a small inset
panels.caption: Theseus walked to Athens. On the road he met villains. That is a different story.
panels.narr: Theseus walks, and beats every bandit on the road. By the time he reaches Athens, everyone knows his name. Everyone except his father.

panels.visual: A palace feast: Theseus at the table taking up his knife, a golden cup beside his plate; Medea in the background, hooded, glaring with glowing eyes
panels.caption: Medea persuaded Aegeus to poison the stranger's cup.
panels.narr: But Medea knows. She wants her own little son to be king. So she tells the old king this famous stranger has come to steal his throne, and hands him the poison.

panels.visual: King Aegeus' hand slaps the golden cup away from the young man's lips; green poison arcs through the air with a tiny skull shape; Medea flees
panels.caption: Aegeus knew that sword. He knocked the cup away.
panels.narr: Theseus draws his sword to cut his meat, on purpose, so his father will see it. Aegeus knows that sword. Medea grabs her boy and runs. That's a myth: Plutarch tells it.

voice_speech.speaker: aegeus
voice_speech.text: Not that cup! My son. My son!

panels.visual: Theseus and Ariadne on a ship sailing away from Crete, bright sea, Theseus smiling, Ariadne leaning on the rail
panels.caption: Ariadne and Theseus sailed away from Crete together.

panels.visual: Ariadne asleep on the beach at Naxos in the dawn light, Theseus's ship leaving the shore far behind
panels.caption: On Naxos he left her asleep on the beach and sailed on.

panels.visual: Ariadne seen from behind, long dark hair whipping in wind, a tiny ship on the far horizon, an inset of her eye with a tear and the ship in it
panels.caption: He left her.

panels.visual: Dionysus the god (garlands, grape-vine crown, smiling kindly) offering Ariadne a hand on the shore, tiger and vines behind him, a bit of colour
panels.caption: Then the god Dionysus found her and married her. Theseus was far away.

panels.visual: The small temple of Athena Nike on its high bastion on the right of the steps up the Acropolis, bright sun, Glauka on the roof
panels.caption: On your right as you climb stands a small temple on a high bastion. Built around 420 BC.

panels.visual: The goddess Nike with big feathered wings flying from one champion to the next, laurel wreath in hand
panels.caption: Nike, goddess of victory, normally has wings. Wings let her fly from one winner to the next.

panels.visual: The wingless statue of Athena Nike on the bastion, athletic, calm, held on the spot by a chain of laurel
panels.caption: In Athens she was shown without wings.

panels.visual: Spartan soldiers marching into a defeated Athens while a tiny Nike flies away over the horizon
panels.caption: Athens lost the war with Sparta anyway. Victory did fly away in the end.

panels.visual: The Odeon of Herodes Atticus: arched stone facade and curved rows, a summer-night concert with musicians and lanterns
panels.caption: A music hall for about five thousand people, built around AD 161.

panels.visual: Herodes Atticus (rich Greek in fine robes, beard) standing in front of his building proudly, a coin purse
panels.caption: Herodes Atticus was the richest man in Greece.

panels.visual: Herodes by a grave wreath with a sad face, the half-built Odeon behind him, dusk
panels.caption: He built it in memory of his wife Regilla. She died while pregnant.

panels.visual: A Roman court with magistrates and Herodes standing calmly while Regilla's brother points at him accusingly
panels.caption: Her brother accused him of ordering it. He was tried in Rome and let off.

panels.visual: A bare mountainside at dusk: a shepherd lifting a tiny baby with bound ankles from a rock; far below the walls of Thebes; a ghostly oracle's vision of a priestess in a mist above
panels.caption: An oracle said the baby prince of Thebes would kill his father and marry his mother. He was left on a mountainside.

panels.visual: On a narrow road the young Oedipus (from the sheet) in a fierce argument with an old man in a chariot who pushes him aside, a rearing horse, dust and speed lines; no gore, the old man shown only shoving
panels.caption: On a narrow road an old man in a chariot pushed him aside. In a rage Oedipus killed him: King Laius, his real father.

panels.visual: The Sphinx (from the sheet: lion body, eagle wings, a woman's face) perched on a high rock above the walls of Thebes, looming over a small group of terrified travellers, eerie moonlight
panels.caption: The Sphinx ate everyone who could not answer her riddle.

speech.speaker: Sphinx
speech.text: What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening?

panels.visual: Close-up of young Oedipus calm and thinking, then a small three-part inset: a crawling baby, a grown man walking, an old man with a stick
panels.caption: Oedipus answered: a human being.

panels.visual: The Sphinx on her rock with wide stunned eyes, wings flaring, then leaping off the cliff in a swirl of feathers and speed lines, tiny Oedipus below looking up; no gore
panels.caption: The Sphinx threw herself off her rock.

panels.visual: A simple royal wedding image: Oedipus crowned as king of Thebes in a red cloak and Queen Jocasta in a purple gown side by side on a throne in front of cheering crowds with flower petals; formal and dignified, nothing romantic
panels.caption: Thebes made Oedipus king, and he married the widowed queen, Jocasta.

panels.visual: The truth revealed: a close-up of Oedipus' shocked face with tiny pupils and sweat drops, Jocasta's pale horrified face behind him; at the corner a small black impact-frame inset showing two raised gold brooches and, from far away, a thin shadow of an empty dangling rope on a wall; no blood
panels.caption: When the truth came out, Jocasta hanged herself. Oedipus blinded himself with her brooches.

panels.visual: The old blind Oedipus with white bandaged eyes and a staff, led gently by his daughter Antigone along a path toward a shady sacred grove of olive trees at Colonus, golden evening light, Glauka in a tree
panels.caption: Led by Antigone, he came to Colonus, and died in a sacred grove. Sophocles was born here.

panels.visual: A calm morning street in Athens: an enslaved man (middle-aged, plain tunic, kind weary face) walking beside a well-dressed boy of about 9, carrying the boy's wax writing tablets and a lyre case, the boy chattering
panels.caption: Rich Athenian boys did not walk to school alone. An enslaved man called a paidagogos, a child-leader, walked beside them and carried their writing tablets.

panels.visual: A classroom of boys sitting on stools learning to read and play the lyre, and at the back, on the floor by the wall, the paidagogos sitting quietly with the tablets on his knee, keeping watch; a stern teacher at the front
panels.caption: He sat in on lessons and made the boys behave.

panels.visual: The boy grown up into a young man in a fine cloak, standing beside the old paidagogos who is now grey-haired, the young man putting a hand on his shoulder, warm light; a thought bubble of the two of them walking as before
panels.caption: Many boys spent more time with their paidagogos than with their own fathers.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl with a little academic cap and a pointer standing next to a big chalkboard-like tablet with the word PEDAGOGUE in large letters; a small inset of an Athenian girl learning to read at home from her mother with a scroll
panels.caption: Our word pedagogue, a teacher, comes from him. Most Athenian girls learned at home, if they learned to read.

panels.visual: The Palamidi fortress on a cliff above Nafplio and its bay, many stone steps zigzagging up, sunny
panels.caption: The Palamidi fortress, built by the Venetians between about 1711 and 1714.

panels.visual: A tour guide with a flag saying '999 steps!' pointing up, tourists with sweaty faces, sun hats
panels.caption: Everyone says there are 999 steps.

panels.visual: A boy counting steps with a clicker, a sweat drop, a long staircase going up out of frame
panels.caption: People who actually counted get different numbers.

panels.visual: Several people each holding a number sign: 850, 920, 999, 1,000, arguing, Glauka looking amused
panels.caption: Usually between about 850 and 1,000, depending on where you start and stop.

panels.visual: The completed Parthenon in bright painted colours (blue, red and gold pediments) glowing on the Acropolis, crowds of Athenians below, Glauka the owl in the sky
panels.caption: The Parthenon, built between 447 and 432 BC, when Pericles led Athens.
panels.narr: The Parthenon went up between 447 and 432 BC, when Pericles led Athens. All Athens came to stare. Somewhere in this crowd is the man in charge. Soon they'll call him a thief.

panels.visual: Pericles (helmet pushed up on his head) points proudly up at the half-built temple while workers haul marble on ropes
panels.caption: Pericles led Athens.
panels.narr: Pericles led Athens, and he wanted the finest temple in Greece. He also had enemies. If they couldn't hit him, they would hit his friends.

panels.visual: Interior view: a gigantic twelve-metre statue of Athena in gold and ivory, helmet and spear, towering over tiny worshippers; ray of light
panels.caption: Inside stood Athena, twelve metres tall, gold and ivory.
panels.narr: Inside stood Athena, twelve metres tall, in gold and ivory. Her gold weighed about a tonne, and it belonged to the city. People would keep an eye on it.

panels.visual: A sculptor with a chisel and a hammer (Phidias, balding, strong forearms) proudly stepping back from the statue's foot
panels.caption: Made by the sculptor Phidias.
panels.narr: She was made by the sculptor Phidias, the best in Greece and a close friend of Pericles. That friendship was about to cost him.

panels.visual: Dramatic diagram-like drawing of the Parthenon with exaggerated curves: the floor bulging up in the middle, columns swelling and leaning inward, thin red guide lines, Glauka pointing with a wing
panels.caption: Almost no straight lines in the whole building.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: The floor rises in the middle!

panels.narr: Phidias was in charge of the whole building. Watch this bit. Look closely: there are almost no straight lines in it.

panels.visual: Close-up of a column swelling in the middle, tape measure and an amazed builder
panels.caption: The columns swell and lean slightly inward.
panels.narr: The columns swell in the middle and lean slightly inward. Look at the builder's face. He has just measured it twice.

panels.visual: The Parthenon from far away looking perfectly straight, a tiny girl-shaped visitor in the foreground squinting
panels.caption: From a distance it looks perfectly straight.
panels.narr: From a distance your eye straightens out the curves, so the whole temple looks perfectly straight. Someone planned every one of those bends.

panels.visual: The Parthenon painted in vivid colours (blue, red, gold) compared with a ghostly white modern version drawn in thin outline on the side
panels.caption: It was painted in bright colours, not the white we see now.
panels.narr: Its carvings were painted in bright colours too, red and blue, not the white we see now. This was the work of the man they called a thief.

panels.visual: A crowd of angry Athenian officials in the Agora pointing at Phidias, who stands calm, arms folded, a scroll of accusation on the floor
panels.caption: Phidias was accused of stealing the gold.
panels.narr: Then the blow fell. One of his own workmen, Menon, went to the market-place and accused Phidias of stealing gold from Athena's statue.

panels.visual: Phidias cleverly unlocking the gold robe plates from the statue of Athena, plates lying in a neat pile
panels.caption: He had built the statue so the gold could be lifted off and weighed.
panels.narr: Phidias didn't argue. Years before, on Pericles' advice, he had built the statue so the gold could be lifted off and weighed. Plate by plate, it came down.

panels.visual: A huge pair of scales with the gold plates on one side and a weight on the other, officials leaning in with eyes popping out of their heads
panels.caption: They weighed it.
panels.narr: They weighed it.

panels.visual: Phidias grinning smugly with arms folded; the scale perfectly balanced; officials with embarrassed sweat drops
panels.caption: It was all there.
panels.narr: Every scrap was there. So his enemies found another charge; Plutarch says Phidias died in prison. That's a legend: a real man, and a story that grew around him. His curves are still here.

panels.visual: Pericles on the Pnyx speaking to a crowd of Athenians with a raised hand, citizens voting with raised hands
panels.caption: For about thirty years, from 461 to 429 BC, Pericles was the leading man of Athens.

panels.visual: Pericles pointing at the rising Parthenon and Propylaia on the Acropolis, builders at work
panels.caption: Pericles persuaded Athens to build the Parthenon and the Propylaia.

panels.visual: A comic poet laughing on a stage as he points at Pericles' very long head under the helmet, an onion floating above, the crowd laughing
panels.caption: Comic poets joked that the helmet hid his strangely long head. They called him onion-head.

panels.visual: A crowded city in the grip of the plague, a mournful Pericles at a doorway, shadows, no bodies shown, only sorrow
panels.caption: In 430 BC a terrible plague struck. His two sons died of it, and in 429 BC so did he.

panels.visual: Prince Hippolytus hunting in the forest with a bow, laughing, a statue of Artemis in the trees; in the distance a small statue of Aphrodite turned away
panels.caption: Hippolytus loved hunting and the goddess Artemis. He had no time for Aphrodite.

panels.visual: Aphrodite (glowing, beautiful, cold) smiling cruelly in the clouds and pointing her finger at Phaedra, a pink glow curse
panels.caption: Aphrodite took her revenge.

panels.visual: Phaedra sitting alone by a window, troubled, a love-struck face, a sad shadow
panels.caption: She made Phaedra fall desperately in love with her own stepson.

panels.visual: Hippolytus turning away from Phaedra in disgust, Phaedra stunned, hurt, a dark tragedy mood
panels.caption: Hippolytus was disgusted and refused her.

panels.visual: A letter on a table, Phaedra's hand with a quill, the dark window; she is gone, only a fluttering curtain, a heavy tragic mood, nothing violent shown
panels.caption: Phaedra left a letter blaming him for something he had not done.

panels.visual: Theseus reading the letter with a stormy face, raising a fist to the sea, waves crashing
panels.caption: Theseus believed the letter and cursed his son with a wish Poseidon had promised him.

panels.visual: On a rocky shore a monstrous bull bursts out of a towering wave in front of a young prince's chariot: horses rearing in panic, spray and speed lines, no gore
panels.caption: A gift from the sea.

panels.visual: Theseus kneeling by the dying Hippolytus with Artemis appearing in silver light behind them, father and son forgiving each other, soft end
panels.caption: Artemis told Theseus the truth. Theseus had learned the truth too late, again.

panels.visual: Aristotle (dandy, rings, neat beard, fine cloak) crouching in a sunny garden with a notebook, carefully watching two real cats washing and stalking
panels.caption: Aristotle watched real cats.

panels.visual: Plato gazing dreamily upward at a glowing, golden, perfect, ideal cat floating in the clouds, hands clasped, while Aristotle in the corner rolls his eyes
panels.caption: Plato dreamed of the perfect cat.

panels.visual: Aristotle counting a cat's whiskers and measuring its paw with a ruler, notes and sketches of birds, plants and a weathervane around him
panels.caption: Count, compare, take them apart.

panels.visual: Aristotle in the Lyceum surrounded by animals, plants, weather charts and scrolls on politics, an exuberant scholar, Glauka the owl on a shelf
panels.caption: He studied animals, plants, weather and politics.

panels.visual: Aristotle at a writing table with his young son Nicomachus (a small boy with curly hair) leaning on his arm, both reading a scroll
panels.caption: He wrote a book on how to live well, named after his son Nicomachus.

panels.visual: A big unrolled scroll with the title NICOMACHEAN ETHICS and the words HOW TO LIVE WELL, light shining from it
panels.caption: The Nicomachean Ethics.

panels.visual: A tree in full blossom with golden fruit and white flowers growing from a scroll, a big word EUDAIMONIA on a ribbon
panels.caption: The goal of life is eudaimonia: flourishing.

speech.speaker: Aristotle
speech.text: Flourish by being good at being human.

panels.visual: Medieval scholars in hooded robes bowing deeply before a tall stack of Aristotle's books on a desk, candlelit monastery library, centuries passing as a calendar
panels.caption: For over a thousand years people believed what he wrote.
