panels.visual: Aristotle explaining with a lead ball and a wooden ball held up in each hand, a thought-bubble of the lead ball falling first; a tick next to it, it looks right
panels.caption: He wrote that heavy things fall faster than light ones. It sounds right.

panels.visual: A tall church tower in Delft in 1586 with Simon Stevin (Flemish engineer, ruff collar, beard) on the top holding two lead balls over the parapet, a friend waiting far below with a hand cupped to his ear
panels.caption: In 1586 Simon Stevin dropped two lead balls from a church tower in Delft.

panels.visual: Two lead balls, one big and one small, falling side by side from the tower with speed lines, the friend below with eyes shut listening, a single big sound-effect
panels.caption: They hit the ground together. A thousand years earlier John Philoponus had already doubted Aristotle.

panels.visual: A small old Italian scholar (Galileo, in a doctor's robe) on the Leaning Tower of Pisa dropping balls, dotted memory-frame, a question mark and a stamp
panels.caption: The Galileo and Pisa story may never have happened. Galileo did prove it with balls rolling down slopes.

panels.visual: Plato (broad-shouldered wrestler, neat beard, rich cloak) and two girls in white chitons (red bow and lilac bow) kneeling in the sand in the Academy grove each drawing a circle with a stick, concentrating
panels.caption: Draw me a perfect circle.

panels.visual: Close-up of three wobbly circles drawn in the sand, each a little lumpy, the stick, footprints, a comic sweat drop
panels.caption: Every circle is a little wobbly.

panels.visual: Plato pointing upwards: in the golden sky a perfect shining glowing circle, with a bright halo, the girls gazing up amazed with mouths open
panels.caption: Yet you know exactly what a perfect circle is.

panels.visual: A cave-like picture: prisoners of the cave watching flickering shadows on the wall, while above, a bright shining perfect circle, a triangle and a heart glow in a sunlit opening; Plato's hand pointing
panels.caption: The Forms are above. Everything we see is only a shadow.

speech.speaker: Plato
speech.text: Everything we see is a shadow of the Forms.

panels.visual: Students in the Academy grove with compasses, triangles and diagrams scratched in the sand, a lively geometry lesson
panels.caption: Plato loved geometry.

panels.visual: Plato holding a drawn perfect triangle that glows above his hand, students looking amazed, thought bubble of a shining shape
panels.caption: Perfect shapes you can only think, never touch.

speech.speaker: Plato
speech.text: It trains the mind to see past the shadows.

panels.visual: A sign over the door of a school reading LET NO ONE IGNORANT OF GEOMETRY ENTER, a student reading it with a gulp
panels.caption: A story says a sign over the door read this.

panels.visual: A long shelf of dusty old books with a timeline arrow showing 900 years, a very late writer holding a quill, and Plato with a raised eyebrow
panels.caption: Nobody mentions it until about nine hundred years after he died.

panels.visual: Travelling sophists in fine robes teaching a crowd of rich young men in the Agora, each with a heavy bag of coins at his feet, confident smirks
panels.caption: Sophists travelled from city to city teaching young men to win arguments, for money.

panels.visual: Two sophists side by side with price tags hanging from their lecterns: one tag reads 100 MINAS (a huge pile of coin bags), the other reads 5 MINAS (a small bag)
panels.caption: Protagoras was said to charge a hundred minas. Evenus charged five.

panels.visual: Socrates (ugly, bald, bushy beard, barefoot, shabby cloak) holding out empty open hands with a cheerful grin, a tiny price tag showing 0 and an empty pouch
panels.caption: Socrates charged nothing, and he had nothing.

speech.speaker: Socrates
speech.text: I charged nothing, and I had nothing.

panels.visual: Socrates looking up at a very confident pompous sophist with a raised chin, a big question mark floating between them
panels.caption: He would ask a simple question.

panels.visual: The pompous sophist answers with a grand gesture and a speech scroll, young men watching, a mood of confidence
panels.caption: The sophist answered confidently.

panels.visual: Socrates with a finger raised asking another question, a chain of question marks, the sophist's smirk beginning to slip, a sweat drop
panels.caption: Then another question, and another.

panels.visual: The sophist tangled in his own words, hair standing up, eyes spinning, a knot of scribbled lines above his head, sweat drops flying; young men in the background laughing
panels.caption: Until he contradicted himself in front of everyone.

panels.visual: The Oracle at Delphi (the Pythia on a golden tripod in swirling mist) declaring in glowing light, Socrates confused in the foreground
panels.caption: The oracle called him the wisest man in Athens.

speech.speaker: Pythia
speech.text: No one is wiser than Socrates.

panels.visual: Socrates tapping his own chest with a gentle smile while behind him a row of pompous Athenians each stand with a thought bubble full of 'I know'
panels.caption: The only reason: he did not think he knew what he did not know. Everyone else did.

speech.speaker: Socrates
speech.text: I don't think I know what I don't know.

panels.visual: A general on a hillside tricking the enemy: a decoy campfire and a hidden army, the general smiling slyly; Socrates and the young Euthydemus watching in an inset
panels.caption: Is deceiving always wrong? A general who tricks the enemy?

panels.visual: A father hiding bitter medicine in a spoon of honeyed food to feed his sick son in bed, the boy trusting, the father tender
panels.caption: A father who tricks his sick son into taking medicine?

panels.visual: A sad man sitting with his head in his hands in a dim room; his friend gently lifting a sword away from the table and holding it behind his back, tender, the sad man not harmed, mood quiet and kind
panels.caption: A man who takes a desperate friend's sword away?

panels.visual: Plato teaching students in a shady olive grove with a sacred shrine, scrolls and a drawing in the dust
panels.caption: Around 387 BC Plato started a school in a grove sacred to the hero Akademos. So it was called the Academy.

panels.visual: A modern city park with ruins and a tall apartment building behind, Glauka perched on a broken column
panels.caption: Every academy in the world since then is named after that grove.

panels.visual: Plato's bare shoulders in a wrestling match in a gym, sand, a crowd, comic scene with 'Platon' meaning broad
panels.caption: Platon means broad. Some say it came from his shoulders.

panels.visual: A sign above a school door reading LET NO ONE IGNORANT OF GEOMETRY ENTER, a student reading it, a question mark and a clock showing centuries
panels.caption: Nobody mentioned that sign until centuries later.

panels.visual: The priestess of Athena Polias (older woman in a long white robe and veil, regal) holding a key and standing by the temple door
panels.caption: The priestess of Athena Polias: the most important religious office in Athens. A woman held it for life.

panels.visual: A priestess shown in four ages as a young woman, middle-aged, older, then elderly, always at the same temple, a counter of 64
panels.caption: Lysimache served for sixty-four years.

panels.visual: Athenian women in their houses at home, a girl of about fourteen at a wedding, a husband leading her away, subdued and sad mood
panels.caption: Women could not vote or own much property, and girls were often married at about fourteen.

panels.visual: A carved stone slab with the priestess' name cut into it, hand tracing the letters, next to a crowd of nameless silhouettes
panels.caption: She was one of the few women whose name was carved on monuments. Most women's names were never written down.

panels.visual: A roadside house on the road to Athens at dusk, an iron bed, and a grinning huge host Procrustes inviting a traveller in
panels.caption: On the road to Athens lived a man called Procrustes. He offered travellers a bed for the night.

panels.visual: A lanky traveller lying on a short iron bed with his feet hanging off and Procrustes looming with a mallet, a sweat drop
panels.caption: If a guest was too short, he stretched him. If too tall, he chopped off his legs.

panels.visual: Procrustes, a hulking grinning villain with an axe, looms over his iron bed in a dark room; the young hero Theseus in the lit doorway in silhouette, sword in hand, long shadow; no blood
panels.caption: Then Theseus came down the road.

panels.visual: A quiet empty road at sunrise with the iron bed abandoned and Theseus walking away, tiny
panels.caption: We still say a Procrustean bed: forcing everything to fit one rule.

panels.visual: The great gateway of the Acropolis, the Propylaia, with its white columns and a steep ramp of steps, Glauka the owl flying through
panels.caption: The Propylaia, the great gateway to the Acropolis. Begun in 437 BC.

panels.visual: Close-up of a wall block with a stone knob sticking out, ropes looped around it, workers hoisting
panels.caption: The builders left knobs so ropes could be looped round for lifting.

panels.visual: A mason with a chisel looking up at a row of knobs, thinking of the plan to chisel them all off
panels.caption: Later they meant to chisel every knob off.

panels.visual: The gateway in 432 BC: tools dropped, workers leaving, messengers on horseback shouting 'War with Sparta!', the knobs still on the blocks
panels.caption: In 432 BC war with Sparta was coming and the work stopped. The knobs are still there.

panels.visual: Pyrrho (lean, serene, travel-worn) marching with Alexander the Great's army across a dusty Indian landscape, elephants and banners, a row of calm sages sitting cross-legged in plain wraps under a tree in the background
panels.caption: Pyrrho marched with Alexander all the way to India and met wise men who sat perfectly calm.

panels.visual: A jar of honey with a spoon and Pyrrho tasting it with a thoughtful face, a thought bubble reading 'seems sweet'
panels.caption: Is honey sweet? It seems sweet to me.

speech.speaker: Pyrrho
speech.text: That is all I can say.

panels.visual: Pyrrho sitting in a peaceful garden with a smile, glowing calm, floating word ATARAXIA on a ribbon, his worry-lines fading, followers listening
panels.caption: Once he stopped insisting he knew, he stopped worrying. Peace of mind: ataraxia. They were the Sceptics.

panels.visual: Pyrrho cheerfully strolling straight towards a cliff edge with a dreamy smile while two worried friends grab his cloak and haul him back, a drop in the background
panels.caption: Stories say friends had to pull him back from cliffs and carts.

panels.visual: Pyrrho calmly walking across a street into the path of a rolling cart, a driver shouting and two friends diving to pull him aside, comic speed lines
panels.caption: And from carts.

panels.visual: A ship in a violent storm at sea with everyone on deck panicking, waving arms, clutching the mast, huge waves, and in the middle a fat pig calmly eating from a trough, comic
panels.caption: In a storm at sea everyone panicked.

panels.visual: Close-up of the pig chewing with a ridiculously serene half-closed-eyes expression while Pyrrho points at it with a big smile, a halo of calm around the pig
panels.caption: Pyrrho pointed at a pig calmly eating on deck.

panels.visual: Pyrrho shrugging with open hands and a small smile, a scroll with a question mark, and behind him a thin ghost image of a sensible man walking along a safe road
panels.caption: Other old writers said he lived sensibly and the cliff stories were jokes.

speech.speaker: Pyrrho
speech.text: I cannot be sure. Neither can you.

panels.visual: Socrates sitting in a small shoemaker's shop in the Agora arguing with young men, Simon the shoemaker working at his bench
panels.caption: I liked to talk with young men at Simon's shoe shop.

panels.visual: Plato and Xenophon (two young men with scrolls) writing in a notebook, Socrates in the background with empty hands
panels.caption: I never wrote a word down. My pupils Plato and Xenophon did.

panels.visual: Archaeologists brushing the dust off hobnails and bone eyelets and a clay cup base with SIMONOS scratched on it
panels.caption: They found iron hobnails and the base of a cup marked SIMONOS: 'Simon's'.

panels.visual: Socrates answering a student's question with another question, a chain of question marks, the student pulling his hair out
panels.caption: I never answered a question straight.

panels.visual: Serious, sober tone: a line of war captives, men, women and children in plain rags, arriving in the Athenian Agora under a heavy sky, led by a trader with a stick held low; faces tired and dignified, no cruelty shown, Glauka watching from a column
panels.caption: In classical Athens perhaps a third of the people were enslaved. Many were captives of war, or bought from slave traders.

panels.visual: A split scene of everyday labour: a girl fetching water in a jar from a fountain house, an enslaved man at a potter's wheel in a workshop, and a man keeping accounts on a wax tablet, quiet muted mood
panels.caption: Some worked in houses, shops and workshops, fetched water or kept accounts.

panels.visual: The Laurion silver mines: a dark cramped tunnel with low stone ceilings lit by tiny oil lamps, exhausted miners crouched with picks, deep shadows, heavy oppressive mood, no violence shown
panels.caption: The worst fate was the silver mines at Laurion, where thousands worked in cramped tunnels underground, often until they died.

panels.visual: Split panel: top, shining silver owl coins and a fleet of Athenian warships (triremes) at Salamis in 480 BC; bottom, citizens raising their hands to vote on the Pnyx hill while a small group of enslaved people stand outside the crowd at the edge, looking on
panels.caption: Laurion's silver paid for the warships at Salamis and the owl coins. Athens' glory rested partly on people who had no vote and no freedom.

panels.visual: Socrates (ugly, bald, bushy beard, barefoot, shabby cloak) in the Agora cheerfully asking a puzzled merchant questions, question marks flying
panels.caption: In 399 BC, Socrates asked awkward questions.
panels.narr: This barefoot old man is Socrates. For years he wandered this Agora asking awkward questions. The poor man on the right only wanted to sell a pot.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: But what is justice? You must know, surely?

panels.visual: Grumpy Athenians in a crowd with arms folded glaring at Socrates, angry shadows
panels.caption: People did not always like the answers.
panels.narr: People did not always like the answers. Socrates showed important men, in public, that they didn't know what they thought they knew. Important men remember that.

panels.visual: A courtroom of 501 jurors in rows, shown as a vast crowd of faces, Socrates standing alone in the centre
panels.caption: He was accused of disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young.
panels.narr: In 399 BC they took him to court. He was accused of disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young. Five hundred and one jurors. One old man, alone in the middle.

panels.visual: A juror's black pebble dropped in an urn, closer view, tension, Socrates' calm face in the background
panels.caption: Five hundred and one citizens found him guilty.
panels.narr: Each juror dropped a pebble. Not all of them voted guilty, but most did: if about thirty had changed their minds, he'd have gone home. Look at his face. Calm.

panels.visual: Socrates in a prison cell with a small barred window and a stone bed, his friends (Crito, a grey-haired man in a plain brown cloak, and two young men; no one in a gold-trimmed cloak) kneeling beside him urging him to leave
panels.caption: His friends offered to help him escape.
panels.narr: His friends offered to help him escape. Crito, his old friend, came to the prison before dawn. The money was ready. Friends far away would hide him.

panels.visual: Close-up of Socrates shaking his head with a kind smile, the old friend Crito's hand on his shoulder
panels.caption: He refused them.
panels.narr: He refused them. All his life he had lived by the laws of Athens. He wasn't going to sneak out of them now, by the back door.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: I will stay. After seventy years, should I run now, Crito?

panels.visual: A servant carrying a clay cup of hemlock on a tray into the cell, grim faces
panels.caption: The sentence was death by poison: hemlock.
panels.narr: The sentence was death by poison: hemlock, made from a plant. A man carried it in. Even the prison guard had cried when he came to say goodbye.

panels.visual: Socrates calmly raising the clay cup, eyes serene above the rim, friends weeping behind him, a small '...'
panels.caption: He drank the cup calmly.
panels.narr: He drank the cup calmly. All of it.

panels.visual: Socrates lying on the bed still talking and gesturing to his friends, who listen in tears
panels.caption: He went on talking about philosophy.
panels.narr: All day he had talked about philosophy with his friends, as if it were any other afternoon. After the cup, he walked about until his legs grew heavy. Then he lay down.

panels.visual: His legs under a blanket, a dimming curve of grey shading creeping up from his feet
panels.caption: The numbness crept up his body.
panels.narr: Socrates couldn't feel his feet when the man pressed them. The numbness crept up his body. His last words were for Crito, about Asclepius, the god of healing.

voice_speech.speaker: Socrates
voice_speech.text: Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay it, won't you?

panels.visual: Young Plato, pale and ill, wrapped in a blanket in a chair at home, writing at a table with a quill and a papyrus by a warm lamp, later, a friend telling him the news
panels.caption: Plato was ill and not there. He wrote it down afterwards.

speech.speaker: Plato
speech.text: I was ill. They told me.

panels.narr: Then he was still. Plato wrote down what happened that day. But Plato wasn't there: he was ill. His friends told him everything.

voice_speech.speaker: Plato
voice_speech.text: I was ill that day. My friends told me everything.

panels.visual: The Agora building in the south-west corner (small, dusty), archaeologists holding up a tiny clay medicine bottle, a big question mark above
panels.caption: It may have been the prison. Nobody can prove it.
panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and here's how we know: Plato. The prison is a best guess: a building in the south-west corner where diggers found tiny clay medicine bottles. Go and find it.

panels.visual: Socrates barefoot in the snow in the same old cloak, a belly, bulging eyes, cheerful, a shivering soldier next to him
panels.caption: My friends said I looked like a satyr: snub nose, bulging eyes. I walked barefoot, even in winter.

panels.visual: Socrates as a stonemason's son with a chisel in a workshop, then as a soldier with a shield, in a split frame
panels.caption: I was a stonemason's son and I fought as a soldier for Athens.

panels.visual: The priestess at Delphi (Pythia) on a tripod in swirling mist, golden glow, saying 'no one is wiser than Socrates', Socrates' face confused
panels.caption: The oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser than me.

speech.speaker: Socrates
speech.text: I know that I know nothing.

panels.visual: Socrates cornering a pompous Athenian with a pile of question marks flying, the Athenian turning red and sweating
panels.caption: I went round asking people what courage, justice and beauty were. It made me very annoying.

panels.visual: Solon (wise old man, wide hat, staff, white beard) on the Pnyx hill speaking to a crowd of Athenian citizens, hand raised, golden light
panels.caption: Around 594 BC, Athens chose Solon to fix its laws.
panels.narr: I have been everywhere, children, and I will tell you all of it. But first: around 594 BC Athens was in a mess, so it chose me, Solon, to fix its laws.

panels.visual: Solon tearing up a scroll of old laws, chains of debtors falling off several Athenians who rejoice
panels.caption: He cancelled most of the old laws and freed Athenians sold as slaves for debt.
panels.narr: Poor Athenians who could not pay their debts were being sold as slaves. I cancelled most of the old laws and set them free. Chains are heavy. Laws should be lighter.

panels.visual: An ancient court and a thief with a single cabbage, a stern judge shouting 'Death!', comic horror
panels.caption: The laws of Draco were so harsh that stealing a cabbage could be punished with death.
panels.narr: Before me, Athens used the laws of Draco. They were so harsh that stealing a cabbage could get you killed. A cabbage! I have met many cabbages. None was worth a man.

panels.visual: A scroll of Draco's laws dripping red ink drawn as 'written in blood', comic, no gore
panels.caption: People said they were written in blood.
panels.narr: People said Draco's laws were written in blood, not ink. Even today you call a cruel rule draconian. Mine were kinder. Kind laws last longer than cruel ones.

panels.visual: Solon travelling on foot along a road with a staff and a travel bag, eagle in the sky
panels.caption: Then Solon travelled.
panels.narr: Then I travelled. I left Athens for ten years, so nobody could make me change my laws. A wise man does not stay home to argue with his own rules.

panels.visual: A glittering hall of treasure: heaps of gold and gems; Croesus, king of Lydia (plump, jewelled, proud) showing off to Solon
panels.caption: Herodotus says he visited Croesus, the richest man in the world.

speech.speaker: Croesus
speech.text: Who is the happiest man alive?

panels.narr: Herodotus says I visited Croesus, king of Lydia, the richest man in the world. His servants showed me every room of his treasure. Then the king asked his question.

voice_speech.speaker: Croesus
voice_speech.text: Tell me, Athenian: who is the happiest man alive?

panels.visual: Croesus leaning forward expecting to hear his own name, big hopeful grin
panels.caption: He expected Solon to say him.
panels.narr: He expected me to say him. Look at that face. A man who asks that question with gold all round him does not want an answer. He wants a mirror.

panels.visual: Solon calmly shaking his head and pointing at a simple Athenian soldier in a distant battle
panels.caption: Solon named an ordinary Athenian who died bravely in battle.

speech.speaker: Solon
speech.text: Call no man happy until he is dead.

panels.narr: I named Tellus, an ordinary Athenian. He had fine sons, saw their children born, and died bravely in battle for his city. Croesus was furious. I told him why.

panels.visual: King Cyrus of Persia and his army overrunning the golden city of Sardis, flames and banners
panels.caption: Years later Croesus lost his kingdom to the Persian king Cyrus.
panels.narr: Years later Croesus lost his kingdom to the Persian king Cyrus. His city, his gold, his throne: all of it gone in one war.

panels.visual: Croesus bound on a high burning pyre, bursting flames, Cyrus watching
panels.caption: He was put on a burning pyre.
panels.narr: Cyrus had him tied up on a great pyre of wood and set it alight. The richest man in the world. All he had left was one sentence.

panels.visual: Croesus' face in a halo of flames shouting a name, desperate
panels.caption: He cried out Solon's name three times.
panels.narr: In the flames, he remembered me.

panels.visual: A sudden rainstorm falling from the sky over the pyre, Cyrus looking up in wonder; in a corner Glauka the owl holds up a tiny wooden sign on which is lettered exactly the word LEGEND? (a question mark after it; the sign does not say Glauka)
panels.caption: A sudden rainstorm put the fire out. But Croesus and Solon may never have met.
panels.narr: Only Apollo's rain could put the fire out. That's a legend: a real person, and a story that grew around him. Croesus became king when Solon was very old. They may never have met.

spartan-fox.title: The Spartan Boy and the Fox

panels.visual: Spartan boys of seven taken from their mothers by a stern soldier, a mother's hand letting go, a crowd of little boys in cloaks
panels.caption: In Sparta, boys were taken from their families at seven to train as soldiers. The system was called the agoge.

panels.visual: Hungry Spartan boys in a dim barracks with thin bowls of porridge, rumbling bellies, determined faces
panels.caption: The boys were kept hungry on purpose.

panels.visual: A boy sneaking up on a market stall to steal an apple, a soldier hiding behind a pillar to watch
panels.caption: They were encouraged to steal food. A boy caught was beaten: for being caught, not for stealing.

panels.visual: A Spartan boy standing perfectly still and silent with a cloak over a bulge, a fox's tail peeking out, sweat on his face, a soldier questioning him; no injury shown
panels.caption: Plutarch tells of a boy who hid a stolen fox cub under his cloak and said nothing rather than be found out.

spartan-shield.title: With Your Shield, or On It

panels.visual: A Spartan mother handing a round bronze shield with a lambda to her young son, stern pride, a hint of tears
panels.caption: When my son goes to war, I hand him his shield.

speech.speaker: Mother
speech.text: Come back with this, or on it.

panels.visual: A line of soldiers carried home on their shields on a funeral march, a mother at the roadside standing straight
panels.caption: Win, or be carried home dead on it.

panels.visual: A fleeing soldier throwing away his shield in panic, a Spartan woman's disapproving face in an inset
panels.caption: Never throw it away to run.

panels.visual: Spartan girls racing, wrestling and learning to be strong; a woman overseeing an estate with scrolls and farm workers
panels.caption: Spartan girls run races and wrestle. Women can own land and run the estates while the men are at war.

stoics-marcus.title: The Emperor Who Was a Stoic

panels.visual: Emperor Marcus Aurelius (bearded, simple cloak over armour) writing in a tent in a military camp by lamplight at night, a scroll and a stylus, soldiers' fires outside
panels.caption: Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, wrote notes to himself in Greek, night after night: the Meditations.

panels.visual: Marcus's hand writing on a scroll with the lamp glow, a swirl of the words beside it, a calm face
panels.caption: You cannot control what others do, only what you do.

panels.visual: Marcus sitting on the edge of a narrow camp bed on a cold morning wrapped in a blanket, grumpy and sleepy, his breath steaming, getting up with effort
panels.caption: On mornings he dreaded, he told himself to get up.

speech.speaker: Marcus
speech.text: Get up. I was made to work with others, like hands and feet.

panels.visual: Athens in AD 176: Marcus on the Acropolis steps pointing at four professors at four lecterns shown as four vignettes in a row: a Platonist with a circle diagram, an Aristotelian with a cat and notebook, a Stoic under a porch and an Epicurean in a garden
panels.caption: In AD 176 he visited Athens and paid for four professors of philosophy.

panels.visual: Wide view of the Theatre of Dionysus on the slope of the Acropolis, rows of ancient Athenians on the hillside, a stage below, sunlit
panels.caption: Theatre was born on this slope.
panels.narr: Theatre was born on this slope, right where you're sitting. I saw the very first plays. Well, from a tree near the top.

panels.visual: Three ancient playwrights (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides) shown side by side as portrait busts with name plaques, each holding a scroll
panels.caption: Plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides had their first performances here.
panels.narr: Three names to know: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. Their plays had their first performances here, on this hillside. Here they are as marble busts. Back then they were writers with a new play.

panels.visual: Thousands of spectators sitting in rows up the hillside, cushions and sunhats, a huge crowd
panels.caption: Up to about sixteen thousand people watched.
panels.narr: Up to about sixteen thousand people watched, once the stone seats were built. They packed the rows with cushions and sunhats. Find the girl with the owl beside her. That's you and me.

panels.visual: The orchestra circle with a chorus of masked men in robes, dancing in a ring, dust rising
panels.caption: Everyone watched from the hillside.
panels.narr: Everyone watched from the hillside while the chorus danced in a ring below, stamping up the dust. Look at their faces: masks, every one. Backstage, one man was getting ready.

panels.visual: Backstage view of three actors holding large masks with painted faces, putting them on
panels.caption: All the actors were men in masks.
panels.narr: All the actors were men in masks. Backstage they pulled on painted faces: a grin, a scowl, a scream. Put one on and you were a king, a slave or a god.

panels.visual: An actor in a queen's mask (woman's face, tragic expression) and a long robe, but with the broad shoulders of a man
panels.caption: Even when they played queens.
panels.narr: Even when they played queens. This one is Hecuba, queen of Troy. Look closely: a woman's face, a long robe and a man's big arms. The audience saw only the queen.

panels.visual: Close-up of the Queen Hecuba mask with a tear painted on it, dramatic stage lighting
panels.caption: Euripides' Hecuba was performed here around 424 BC.
panels.narr: Euripides' Hecuba was performed here around 424 BC. Troy has fallen. Her children are taken from her, one by one. Then the queen weeps.

panels.visual: The empty stage with a clear sign of no women: a crossed-out ladies silhouette in a thought bubble over a puzzled Glauka
panels.caption: No women stood on this stage.
panels.narr: No women stood on this stage. Every queen, every mother, every goddess was a man in a mask. The saddest woman in Troy was played by a man.

panels.visual: The front row of the theatre with marble thrones; the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus in the middle, richly carved
panels.caption: In the front row, in the middle, is the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus.
panels.narr: Now look at the front row, in the middle. That's the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus, the god this whole theatre was built for.

panels.visual: The priest of Dionysus in a rich robe and a wreath sitting comfortably on his throne with a cushion and a drink
panels.caption: He had the best view in the theatre.
panels.narr: He had the best view in the theatre, close enough to see every mask. Look at him: a soft cushion and a cup in his hand.

panels.visual: Modern view of the same throne in ruins on a sunny day with little tourists posing next to it
panels.caption: It is still there.
panels.narr: It is still there, cracked and worn, in the same front row. Tourists stop to photograph it every day. Now you know who sat in it.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl sitting on the arm of the marble throne and facing us proudly
panels.caption: Take your seat.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: The best view in the house.

panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. Euripides' Hecuba still survives, and the priest's seat is still in the front row. Climb higher, look down at the stage, and picture the queen.

panels.visual: A huge Persian army marching along a coast with endless banners, King Xerxes on a golden chariot
panels.caption: In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with a huge army.

panels.visual: The narrow pass of Thermopylae between steep cliffs and the sea with a thin line of Spartan soldiers in red cloaks, round shields, King Leonidas in front
panels.caption: At the narrow pass, Leonidas with three hundred Spartans held them off for three days.

panels.visual: A Persian messenger demanding weapons, Leonidas replying calmly with his spear
panels.caption: Leonidas is said to have answered: come and take them.

panels.visual: A local man, Ephialtes, pointing at a mountain path behind the Greeks, Persian scouts creeping on the high trail, dusk; no violence shown
panels.caption: Ephialtes showed the Persians a path round behind them. The Persians then marched on and burnt Athens.

panels.visual: The Athenians' annual sacred ship setting sail for Delos with garlands, crowds on the harbour waving
panels.caption: Every year the Athenians sailed a ship to the island of Delos for a festival.

panels.visual: Carpenters replacing old rotten planks with new ones, a pile of old planks beside the ship
panels.caption: As the planks rotted, they replaced them, one by one.

panels.visual: A ship with all new planks and a pile of old planks on the shore, a pair of philosophers scratching their heads, a big question mark
panels.caption: Was it still the same ship? Philosophers argued about it.

panels.visual: Socrates in prison watching a harbour through the bars, waiting; a faint ship on the sea in the distance
panels.caption: No execution could take place while the ship was away. Socrates waited about a month.

panels.visual: The grumpy tortoise on the south slope of the Acropolis lifting a bored eyebrow at us
panels.caption: Meet the tortoise. It has heard a story or two.

panels.visual: Aeschylus (bald old tragedian in a robe, writing) in Sicily in the sun, a scroll on his knee
panels.caption: Aeschylus, the first great writer of tragedies, died in Sicily around 456 BC.

panels.visual: A giant eagle carrying a tortoise high above a rocky Sicilian hillside, below a bald man sitting, the sun glinting off his head
panels.caption: The story goes that an eagle mistook the old man's bald head for a rock and dropped the tortoise.

panels.visual: The tortoise close-up with a deadpan face, one eyebrow raised, and a tiny sign reading 'story, not report'
panels.caption: A bald playwright, though? Almost certainly made up.

panels.visual: King Minos on his throne in Knossos, stern, purple robe, double-axe emblem, a golden bull relief behind him
panels.caption: King Minos of Crete: his son Androgeos died in Athens.

panels.visual: Seven boys and seven girls from Athens standing in a line, frightened, drawing lots from a jar held by an official
panels.caption: Every nine years Athens must send seven boys and seven girls, chosen by lot.

panels.visual: The dark Labyrinth entrance at the foot of the palace, torches, a distant huge shadow of a bull-headed giant, young faces
panels.caption: Minos shut them in the Labyrinth, and the Minotaur takes them.

panels.visual: A ship with solid black sails leaving the harbour of Athens, grey sky, families waving from the shore
panels.caption: Their ship sails under black sails. No one has ever come back to change them to white.

panels.visual: The mound of Hisarlik in a field in Turkey, with layers of ruins cut in a trench, Glauka flying over
panels.caption: Troy was a real city, at a place we now call Hisarlik, in Turkey.

panels.visual: Schliemann in the trench holding up a cross-section drawing with nine layered cities, one burning red
panels.caption: Schliemann found nine cities, each built on top of the one before. One layer burned around 1180 BC.

panels.visual: A great siege: ten years of tents around a wall, a question mark over a queen's silhouette (Helen)
panels.caption: Did a Greek army really besiege it for ten years over a queen called Helen? Nobody knows.

panels.visual: Gold jewellery and cups piled in a basket labelled PRIAM'S TREASURE, Schliemann smuggling a box out under a coat; a Russian museum shown in a thought bubble
panels.caption: Schliemann smuggled the gold out of Turkey. It is now in a museum in Moscow.

panels.visual: Greek ships sailing away over the horizon in the morning light and a gigantic wooden horse standing alone on the beach
panels.caption: After ten years the Greeks pretended to give up and left a giant wooden horse on the beach.

panels.visual: Trojan crowds coming out of the gates to look at the horse, children pointing, a celebration atmosphere
panels.caption: It was a gift, they said.

panels.visual: Cassandra (wild dark hair, wide eyes) in front of the horse warning the crowd, nobody listening, a priest Laocoön next to her
panels.caption: Cassandra warned them it would destroy the city. Nobody ever believed Cassandra.

panels.visual: Two huge sea serpents rising from the sea towards the priest Laocoön and his sons on the shore, dramatic waves, no gore shown
panels.caption: A priest called Laocoön warned them too. Sea serpents rose out of the water.

panels.visual: Trojans pulling the horse on ropes and rollers through the gates of Troy, wheels creaking, cheering
panels.caption: The Trojans dragged the horse inside the walls.

panels.visual: A hatch opening in the belly of the horse at night, Greek soldiers' helmets peeping out, moonlight
panels.caption: That night Greek soldiers climbed out of its belly.

panels.visual: The Greek soldiers opening the city gates to let the army in, torches, a sleeping town, a burning tower beginning
panels.caption: They opened the gates and burnt Troy. Odysseus had thought of the trick.

panels.visual: A modern computer screen with a picture of a horse on it and a little hand of a soldier peeking out, Glauka tapping the screen
panels.caption: A Trojan horse is also what we call a computer virus.

panels.visual: The Persian king Xerxes (tall crown, rich robe, fierce) on a throne watching Athens from a hill, his huge army arrayed
panels.caption: In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes captured Athens.

panels.visual: Most Athenians fleeing by ship to the island of Salamis, a long line of boats on the sea at dawn
panels.caption: Most Athenians had fled to the island of Salamis.

panels.visual: Persian soldiers in scale armour in the foreground as the temples on the Acropolis burn behind them; a lone Athenian defender leaps from the wall in silhouette against the flames
panels.caption: Then the Persians burnt the temples.

panels.visual: A small green olive shoot sprouting from a burnt black stump of the sacred olive tree, a ray of light, an amazed Greek looking on
panels.caption: The next day a new shoot a forearm long had grown from the burnt olive tree.

panels.visual: A Cypriot merchant ship with purple dye barrels sinking in a storm, Zeno clinging to a plank
panels.caption: Zeno came from Cyprus as a merchant with a cargo of purple dye. His ship was wrecked.

panels.visual: Zeno in a bookshop in Athens reading a scroll, a bookseller pointing out of the door at a passing philosopher
panels.caption: In a bookshop in Athens he asked where he could find men like Socrates.

panels.visual: The Painted Porch (Stoa Poikile): a long colonnade covered with battle paintings, Zeno teaching a crowd
panels.caption: He taught in the Painted Porch. His followers were called Stoics, after the stoa.

panels.visual: The slave Epictetus with his leg twisted by his master, calm face, a stern master, a sweat drop; no gore
panels.caption: A Stoic called Epictetus, born a slave, said calmly: 'You will break it.' Then: 'Did I not tell you?'
